title: Genome-wide screen reveals dependence of break induced replication on several distinct checkpoints

paper_content.abstract: Break-induced replication (BIR) is a primary homologous recombination pathway for repairing one-ended double-strand DNA breaks, including those arising from collapsed replication forks and eroded telomeres. BIR frequently leads to loss of heterozygosity, genetic mutations, and gross chromosomal rearrangements, all hallmarks of cancer. Here, we conducted a genome-wide screen that allowed us to identify and validate the involvement of 33 novel yeast genes in BIR. We report that, while DNA damage and spindle checkpoint machineries are both required to delay nuclear division and provide adequate time for BIR to complete, the spindle position checkpoint is required to coordinate between nuclear division and cytokinesis. Furthermore, we show that two nucleopore proteins play a sequential role during BIR: Nup84 acts before DNA synthesis, while Nup188 functions later to support repair completion. Given the conservation of BIR between yeast and humans and the role of BIR in cancer development, human homologs of the identified BIR proteins may represent promising targets for anti-cancer therapeutics.
paper_content.introduction:
Break-induced replication (BIR) is a homologous recombination pathway that repairs one-ended DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs), including those formed by telomere erosion and replication fork collapse. During BIR repair, one broken chromosome end primes DNA synthesis using the homologous donor as a template, and this repair synthesis can proceed for hundreds of kilobases (reviewed in refs. 1–4). The BIR replication machinery manifests as a “migrating bubble”, first synthesizing the leading strand, which subsequently serves as the template for lagging strand synthesis; consequently, inheritance of the newly synthesized DNA is conservative 5,6. The unusual mode of DNA synthesis during BIR causes high levels of genetic instabilities such as a mutation rate that is up to 1000 times higher than that of S-phase replication as well as frequent genome rearrangements and copy number variations (CNVs) 5,7–16. BIR has also been proposed as a source of genome instability in humans 2. In particular, BIR can induce segmental duplications found in precancerous cells 17, and, in the presence of DNA-damaging agents, BIR promotes the formation of mutation clusters similar to those observed in cancer 8,18,19. BIR is also responsible for alternative lengthening of telomeres (ALT) (reviewed in refs. 2,20–22) and for mitotic DNA synthesis (MiDAS) 23,24, which respectively maintain telomere length in ~15% of cancers and complete replication of so-called DNA fragile sites that remain unreplicated until mitosis.

Our knowledge of BIR in human cells heavily relies on decades of studies characterizing the pathway in yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae, the organism in which eukaryotic BIR was initially discovered 25–29. Numerous proteins that promote BIR have been identified in yeast through the candidate gene approach. For example, factors involved in BIR synthesis including Pol δ-RFC-PCNA, Pif1, DNA primase-DNA polymerase α, and RPA were all identified in yeast 30–33 and confirmed to be conserved in humans 34,35. Pol32, which is a subunit of Pol δ that is not essential for S-phase DNA replication, is required for BIR 30, as is Pif1 helicase 32, and these two proteins have become important biomarkers to detect BIR in various experimental systems.

The genetic requirements for the first steps of BIR are similar to other homologous repair pathways: BIR is initiated by 5′-to-3′ resection executed by the Mre11-Rad50-Xrs2 complex, then relies on Dna2-Sgs1 helicases and/or Exo1 exonuclease 36–38, followed by the participation of Rad52, Rad51, Rad55, Rad57, and Rad54 to complete the homology search and displacement loop (D-loop) formation 26,28,39. Additionally, Srs2 helicase/translocase plays an important role by counteracting the formation of toxic intermediates that arise from the invasion of long Rad51-bound ssDNA accumulated behind the D-loop into the BIR template 40. Recent studies also revealed that BIR requires several histone modification proteins, including Hst3 and Hst4 histone deacetylases and the histone methyltransferase Dot1 41; however, the full complement of epigenetic enzymes involved in BIR remains unknown. Also, because BIR takes a significant amount of time to complete and usually occurs during G2/M or mitosis, the DNA damage checkpoint (DDC) machinery is required to initiate and maintain cell cycle arrest for BIR synthesis to complete prior to cell division 9,28. Recently, it was discovered that nucleopore proteins Nup84 and Nup60 as well as motor protein Kinesin-14 and the Slx5-Slx8 SUMO-targeted ubiquitin ligase are required for BIR 42–44, suggesting that successful completion of BIR may require relocation of the broken chromosome to the nuclear periphery.

Although the candidate gene approach has generated a notable list of genes that participate in BIR, our knowledge of the factors that contribute to successful execution and to regulation of BIR remains incomplete. To address this gap, in this study, we conducted a whole-genome screen using our new yeast BIR system and the yeast knockout (YKO) collection, which includes mutant strains with knockouts (KOs) of all non-essential genes, to identify new candidate genes required for BIR. As a result of this study, we identified and validated 33 previously unrecognized BIR driver genes encoding proteins in a variety of functional groups—including checkpoint proteins, nuclear pore structural proteins, and proteins involved in post-translational modification of nucleosomes—and subjected several of them to deeper functional analysis. We discovered that, in addition to the DNA damage checkpoint, successful completion of BIR requires coordination between nuclear division and cytokinesis mediated by the spindle assembly checkpoint (SAC) and spindle position checkpoint (SPOC), respectively.
paper_content.results:
Yeast BIR system
We constructed an experimental system in yeast that allows for both quantitative and semi-quantitative assessment of BIR efficiency (Fig. 1a). This system is based on the haploid yeast strain KT556 (Supplementary Data 1), which contains an ADE2 gene and a 5′ portion of LYS2 gene (P-lys) containing an HO endonuclease recognition motif on chromosome V (ChrV) between CAN1 and NPR2. Notably, there are no essential genes located centromere-distal from this HO motif position. We also inserted a 3′ fragment of LYS2 (ys2), which shares 2.3 kb of homology with P-lys, into chromosome III (ChrIII) at the HIS4 locus (Fig. 1a). Addition of galactose to the medium induces GAL::HO endonuclease, leading to a DSB in P-lys that invades ys2 and repair by BIR. Consequently, successful BIR repair can be identified by an Ade-Lys+ phenotype (Fig. 1a).

Following DSB induction, the survival rate in wild-type (WT) cells was 46.5% (Fig. 1b), and 90% of survivors were Ade-Lys+ (~42% BIR efficiency). The chromosome structures of BIR outcomes were confirmed by contour-clamped homogeneous electric field (CHEF) gel electrophoresis followed by Southern blot analysis (Supplementary Fig. 1). Deletion of RAD51, RAD52, POL32, or SRS2, known to be critical BIR genes, significantly decreased BIR efficiency (Fig. 1b and Supplementary Data 2.1). In addition, we determined that BIR efficiency could be efficiently determined by the number of Lys+ papillae formed when replica-plated from complete medium onto synthetic complete medium lacking lysine (SC-Lys) (Fig. 1c), providing a rapid, semi-quantitative test for BIR efficiency. Together, these results indicate that our new ectopic BIR system is suitable for quantitative and semi-quantitative analysis of BIR efficiency.

Whole genome screen for BIR genes
To conduct a genome-wide screen for yeast genes that drive and regulate BIR, we modified our ectopic BIR experimental system by inserting several genetic markers to allow selection for GAL::HO and BIR cassettes, as well as to enable the selection of ectopic outcomes (see “Methods” and Supplementary Fig. 2). The resulting strain was used to perform a genome-wide screen by individual crossing of this MATa strain with strains from the YKO collection containing ~5000 MATα strains with individual non-essential genes disrupted by a KANMX cassette, conferring resistance to G418 (Fig. 1d and Supplementary Fig. 2).

Next, BIR efficiencies in the resulting KO strains were assessed using the semi-quantitative approach (Fig. 1c), where strains were first grown on YEPD plates (see “Methods”) to allow a low level of DSB induction associated with “leaky” expression of the GAL::HO endonuclease, followed by replica plating onto SC-Lys medium (Fig. 1d; “Methods”). We identified 335 KO strains (Supplementary Data 3) with fewer Lys+ papillae compared to WT, 19 of which (e.g. RAD52, RAD51, POL32, SRS2, RAD54;) were already known to promote BIR. From the rest, 92 genes were selected for further characterization based on their known roles in processes related to DNA metabolism, including, for example spindle checkpoints, nucleopore structure, and post-translational modification of proteins associated with DNA (Supplementary Data 3). The other identified genes, including mitochondrial and metabolism/biosynthetic genes (Supplementary Data 3), were expected to affect BIR indirectly and, therefore, were not prioritized in this study.

We re-introduced deletions of 64 of the 92 prioritized genes into our ectopic BIR system (AM3422), and we observed that 30 of these genes were indeed required for BIR (Fig. 1e), as their deletions significantly decreased BIR efficiency (Supplementary Data 2 and 3). In addition, we were able to introduce 24 of these 30 deletions in another ectopic BIR system (YSJ131), and each of these single-gene mutants showed BIR defect (Supplementary Data 2.2); in this system, the HO-induced break occurs in chromosome V, and BIR repair is initiated by invasion into leu2 on chromosome III, followed by 41 kb of repair synthesis 45 (Supplementary Fig. 3a). Twenty-six of the new KO strains did not show any BIR defect (Supplementary Data 2.1), indicating that deletion of these genes likely affected cell growth on SC-Lys without affecting BIR specifically. Interestingly, deletions of the remaining six genes (UBA3, UBA4, MUB1, CCS1, YVH1, and PIB2) resulted in increased BIR efficiency, suggesting these genes represent BIR suppressors; however, these genes were probably selected by our screen due to conferring a slow-growth phenotype (Supplementary Data 3).

Spindle assembly checkpoint genes are required for BIR completion
The major function of the spindle assembly checkpoint (SAC) is to ensure accurate chromosome segregation by monitoring for proper attachment of spindle microtubules to kinetochores. In the presence of unattached or incorrect kinetochore–microtubule attachments, the SAC is activated to delay nuclear division 46,47. Our screen identified a BIR defect in strains with deletion of the SAC genes BUB1 and BUB3, suggesting a role for the SAC in BIR. In support of this hypothesis, we observed a defective BIR in bub1Δ, bub3Δ, and mad2Δ mutants in two ectopic BIR systems (AM3422 and YSJ131; Fig. 2a, b and Supplementary Fig. 3a, b; Supplementary Data 2), However, no defect was observed upon deletion of the SAC gene MAD3 (Fig. 2a and Supplementary Data 2).

To investigate the mechanism by which SAC mutants affect BIR, we deleted SAC genes in our allelic BIR system 48, which is disomic for Chr III (Fig. 2c). In this system, galactose-induced DSBs in a truncated copy of Chr III (recipient) are repaired mainly by BIR using a full-length Chr III (donor) as the homologous template. Successful BIR repair results in copying of ~100 kb of template DNA and yields two full-length copies of Chr III. Auxotrophic markers allow determination of BIR (Leu-Ade+), while gross chromosomal rearrangements (GCRs), which also present phenotypically as Leu-Ade+, are distinguished from BIR by CHEF gel analysis (Supplementary Figs. 4–6). Phenotypes of other repair events are also distinguishable: gene conversion (GC) outcomes are Leu+Ade+; failed repair, including chromosome loss of the truncated Chr III (CL), presents as Leu-Ade-red; and half-crossovers (HCs) resulting from fusions between the recipient and donor chromosomes are characterized by Leu-Ade-white (Fig. 2c). An important feature of this strain is that it is usually viable even when repair fails.

Consistent with our findings in the other systems, BIR was significantly reduced in bub1Δ, bub3Δ, and mad2Δ mutants (Fig. 2d and Supplementary Fig. 4 for CHEF analysis), but not in mad3Δ mutants (Supplementary Data 4). In addition, bub1Δmad2Δ double mutants showed a BIR defect similar to each single mutant (Fig. 2d and Supplementary Data 4; Supplementary Fig. 4a, h). Together, our data support that the SAC plays an important role during BIR.

To determine the specific BIR step that is defective in SAC mutants, we examined the kinetics of BIR using our droplet digital PCR (ddPCR)-based Assay for Monitoring BIR Elongation Rate (AMBER) 49. AMBER showed that, in WT cells 10 h after DSB induction, DNA copy number had increased ~1.5x at the P2 position (~6 kb from the X-region of MAT locus), ~1.4x at P4 (~34 kb away), and ~1.4x at P5 (~65 kb away) (Fig. 2c, e and Supplementary Data 5, 6), in agreement with previous observations 49. However, the increase in copy number at these positions was lower in bub1Δ and mad2Δ than in WT (Fig. 2f, g and see also Fig. 2h for the comparison at P2), indicative of a decrease in BIR synthesis in these mutants.

SAC proteins are required to prolong G2/M arrest during BIR
Because BIR is a slow repair process that can take more than 10 h, the efficiency of BIR heavily relies on DNA damage checkpoint (DDC) activity, which initiates G2/M cell cycle arrest to provide sufficient time for BIR to complete prior to nuclear division 9,28. Based on the hits from our screen, we hypothesized that BIR may also require the SAC to prolong the cell cycle arrest established by the DDC. To test this, we created rad9Δbub1Δ, rad9Δbub3Δ, and rad9Δmad2Δ strains defective for both DDC and SAC activities and compared the effects of these double deletions on DSB repair with those of single ones using the Chr III disomic system. Consistent with previous findings 9, rad9Δ cells showed significantly reduced BIR efficiency, and double mutants with a defective DDC and SAC exhibited an even greater decrease in BIR efficiency (Fig. 3a and Supplementary Fig. 4), supporting our hypothesis that both the DDC and the SAC contribute to successful completion of BIR.

If the SAC is required to extend cell cycle arrest initially established by the DDC, we expected that insufficient SAC activity would shorten the duration of G2/M arrest in cells undergoing BIR, causing SAC mutants to complete nuclear division more rapidly. To test this, we monitored nuclear division in disomic BIR derivative strains using DAPI staining and determined the proportion of cells in different cell cycle phases for 12 h after DSB induction (Fig. 3b). In WT, prior to DSB induction, ~70% (on average) of cells were in G1, while G2/M arrested cells were rare (~6%) (Fig. 3c, i and Supplementary Data 7). Upon DSB induction, the proportion of G2/M cells rapidly increased, reaching a maximum of ~89% by 5 h post-DSB. At the 8-h time point, ~15% of cells had resumed nuclear division, and the fraction of G2/M-arrested cells had decreased, reflecting completion of BIR repair (Fig. 3c, i). Like WT cells, the majority of bub1Δ and mad2Δ cells successfully arrested at G2/M, with the maximum proportion of arrested cells achieved by 5 or 6 h post-DSB (Fig. 3d, e, i and Supplementary Data 7); however, the fraction of G2/M-arrested cells remained lower compared to WT between the 5 h and 8 h time points (Fig. 3i). This suggests that the SAC may play a role—in parallel with the DDC—in the establishment of G2/M arrest, which is consistent with the decrease in BIR synthesis observed by AMBER starting around 6 h post-DSB in SAC mutants (Fig. 2h). Further, resumption of mitosis was earlier as it was observed more frequently in mutants compared to WT cells between the 6.5 h and 8 h time points (Fig. 3j). These findings indicate that BIR requires participation of both the DDC and SAC checkpoints. Specifically, we propose that G2/M checkpoint arrest established in cells undergoing BIR repair is extended by the SAC, and that this is important for BIR completion.

To explore whether the SAC may contribute to the establishment of G2/M arrest in the absence of a functional DDC, we microscopically analyzed rad9Δ cells as well as rad9Δbub1Δ and rad9Δmad2Δ double mutants. In rad9Δ cells, the fraction of G2/M cells reached ~28% by 4 h post-DSB and a maximum of ~41% by 7 h post-DSB (Fig. 3f, k), demonstrating that these cells could undergo a partial G2/M arrest, consistent with previous reports 9. In rad9Δbub1Δ and rad9Δmad2Δ cells, the proportion of cells in G2/M remained low throughout the time course and was significantly lower compared to rad9Δ cells (Fig. 3g, h, k and Supplementary Data 7), supporting that checkpoint-mediated cell cycle arrest was abolished in the double mutants and suggesting that the partial G2/M arrest in rad9Δ is driven by SAC machinery. Overall, we propose that, in addition to prolonging a DDC-induced G2/M cell cycle arrest, the SAC can mediate the establishment of cell cycle arrest in response to a DSB in the context of both a functional and a defective DDC.

The spindle position checkpoint is essential for BIR
Given that BIR proceeds during an extended G2/M arrest, wherein the undivided nuclei are positioned at the bud neck, we posited that BIR may also require the spindle position checkpoint (SPOC; reviewed in ref. 50) to block mitotic exit until the nucleus migrates into the bud after BIR is completed. To test the dependence of BIR on the SPOC, we deleted the main SPOC gene, BUB2 in two ectopic BIR systems, one of which required 65 kb (AM3422) and the other required 41 kb (YSJ131) of repair synthesis to complete BIR and observed that deleting BUB2 led to decreased BIR efficiency in both systems (Supplementary Fig. 3a–c). In the allelic (disomic) system, the kinetics of BIR synthesis measured by AMBER in a bub2Δ mutant was similar to that observed in the SAC mutants (Figs. 2h and 4a, b). However, strikingly, bub2Δ mutants exhibited significantly low viability after the DSB in this disomic system, in which a BIR defect normally does not lead to cell death (Fig. 4c and Supplementary Data 4): only 4% of bub2Δ cells survived after the DSB compared to > 95% viability in WT and SAC mutants. Microscopic examination demonstrated that, following plating on YEP-Gal medium, most bub2Δ cells divided no more than 2-3 times, and no cells formed micro-colonies after DSB induction (Supplementary Fig. 3d), confirming lethality following the DSB. A similar striking loss of viability after BIR induction was observed when BFA1, another SPOC gene encoding a partner of Bub2 51,52, was deleted (Fig. 4c). In addition, genetic analysis demonstrated that both SPOC mutants exhibited a decreased fraction of BIR outcomes among the rare survivors and a significant increase in GC outcomes (Fig. 4d and Supplementary Fig. 5), which concludes faster than BIR and usually does not trigger checkpoint arrest in the allelic system 28. However, in an ectopic system (YSJ133) 45, where the homology search takes longer and even GC can trigger checkpoint arrest BUB2 deletion led to a modest decrease in GC efficiency (Supplementary Fig. 3b), but the defect of BIR in this system (YSJ131) 45 was more severe (Supplementary Fig. 3b). The fraction of HC outcomes among survivors was very low in bub2Δ and bfa1Δ mutants (Fig. 4d), likely because of the extended time required for HC formation, which involves secondary breakage of the donor chromosome. Collectively, these results support that the viability of cells undergoing BIR depends on the SPOC.

To determine the mechanism underlying the dependence of cells on the SPOC during BIR repair, we monitored nuclear divisions in SPOC mutants. We observed that, similarly to SAC mutants, bub2- and bfa1-deficient cells started recovery from G2/M arrest earlier, at 5–6 h after DSB induction (Fig. 4e–g, i and Supplementary Fig. 3e), compared to WT. Notably, though, starting from 6 h, SPOC mutants accumulated cells with a unique morphology: they re-budded and formed “chained” cells (usually groups of 3 cells) containing only one undivided nucleus (Fig. 4e–g, j). We propose that the premature re-budding and cell death result from the inability of SPOC-deficient cells to delay their cytokinesis in response to the nuclear division arrest caused by the DDC and SAC. Indeed, deletion of MAD2 in bub2Δ mutants led to earlier escape from G2/M arrest after DSB induction (Fig. 4h, i). Consequently, compared to bub2Δ, the double mutants showed a significantly decreased occurrence of “chained” cells (Fig. 4j), increased cell viability (Fig. 4c), and a higher fraction of interrupted BIR outcomes, including HC and CL among survivors, making the double mutants phenotypically similar to mad2Δ (Figs. 2d and 4d). Altogether, these results support our hypothesis that coordination between nuclear division and cytokinesis is critical for the success of BIR and for viability of cells undergoing BIR. Consistent with this notion, three other genes involved in nuclear migration (JNM1, NUM1, and ARP1) 53,54 and known to have genetic interactions with SPOC genes 55 were identified in this BIR screen and validated as genes required for BIR in our ectopic system (AM3422; Supplementary Fig. 3f).

Differential roles of inner and outer ring nuclear pore proteins in BIR
It has been proposed that, similar to other DSB repair events that take a significant amount of time for completion, BIR requires chromosomes to re-locate to a nuclear pore to execute repair (reviewed in ref. 56). NUP84, encoding a component of the outer nuclear pore ring, was previously reported to be important for BIR 42,43, but the precise step of BIR where it functions has not been determined. In addition, our screen identified a dependency of BIR on NUP188, which encodes a protein of the inner ring of nuclear pores 56.

To increase our understanding of the role of nuclear pore proteins during BIR, we compared nup188Δ and nup84Δ mutants and found that both mutants exhibited a BIR defect in our ectopic system (Supplementary Fig. 6a). In the allelic system, loss of either gene also led to profound BIR defects; however, the specific phenotypes following DSB induction observed in these two mutants differed from each other. Specifically, in nup84Δ, the fraction of Leu-Ade+ outcomes was decreased and the frequency of defective DSB repair (i.e., CL) was increased, while cell viability remained high and similar to WT (Fig. 5a, b). In addition, CHEF analysis demonstrated that a very large fraction (32%) of Leu-Ade+ outcomes in nup84Δ cells represented GCRs (Supplementary Fig. 6b, c), supportive of a BIR defect in the absence of Nup84. Moreover, based on AMBER, even initiation of BIR synthesis was defective in nup84Δ, with virtually no DNA copy number increase at any of the probe positions (Fig. 5c, e; compared to WT in Fig. 5d and Supplementary Fig. 6h).

To test the hypothesis that broken DNA ends may physically relocate to nuclear pores, we performed chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP), which showed that Nup84 accumulates at the DSB position 4 h after the break, and diminishes by 10 h (Fig. 5g). Next, using an anti-Rad51 antibody, we observed a WT level of Rad51 accumulation at the DSB in the absence of Nup84, suggesting that DSB resection and Rad51 loading proceed normally in the absence of Nup84 (Fig. 5h). Further, we used donor-specific primers that recognized a sequence 100 bp telomere-proximal to MAT, and we found that Rad51 loading on the donor (indicative of strand invasion) was decreased ~2 fold but still occurred in the absence of Nup84 (Fig. 5h). From these findings, we propose that while Nup84 facilitates strand invasion, and possibly the homology search, its essential role is in the next step of recombination, which could include D-loop stabilization and/or initiation of DNA repair synthesis.

Our results suggested that Nup188 acts later during BIR than Nup84. Specifically, AMBER showed that nup188Δ had only a very slight defect in the initial steps of BIR synthesis but a very dramatic defect at the end of synthesis (Fig. 5f and Supplementary Fig. 6h). We also found that nup188Δ had drastically decreased viability compared to WT (12% vs. 96%, respectively) but did not have a significant increase of GCRs among Leu-Ade+ outcomes (Fig. 5a, b and Supplementary Fig. 6b, d). We found that nup188Δnup84Δ double mutants had higher viability than nup188Δ (78% vs 12%, respectively) (Fig. 5a) and an altered distribution of DSB repair outcomes (Fig. 5b and Supplementary Fig. 6b, g), supporting our hypothesis that Nup188 participates later than Nup84 in BIR. In addition, it has been shown that human homolog of yeast Nup188 (hNUP188) interacts with centrosomes, the functional counterpart of spindle pole body 57, suggesting that Nup188 could be involved in checkpoint regulation. In support of this, the fractions of DSB repair outcomes that take a significant amount of time to complete (including, HC, and CL) were decreased in nup188Δ (Fig. 5b), similar to SPOC mutants. Additional support came from the observation that deleting MAD2 or RAD9 in nup188Δ significantly increased viability after DSB induction, albeit BIR remained defective (based on the distribution of repair outcomes) (Fig. 5a, b and Supplementary Fig. 6b, e, f). Together, we characterized the important role played by Nup84 during BIR initiation and identified Nup188 as a protein that is important for the successful completion of BIR.

Epigenetic modifiers regulate BIR
The discovery that histone deacetylases Hst3 and Hst4 and histone methyltransferase Dot1 are important for BIR 41 revealed the importance of histone modifications in BIR, even though their exact role in regulating BIR remains unclear. Our screen identified genes encoding both known (Dot1) and previously unrecognized protein-modifying enzymes that are required for high BIR efficiency, including proteins involved in acetylation, deacetylation, methylation, ubiquitination, and urmylation (Fig. 6a and Supplementary Fig. 7a; Supplementary Data 2, 3). While the specific substrates affected by these proteins during BIR will be explored in future studies, our initial analysis suggests that multiple pathways and complex mechanisms are involved.

Based on characterization of hits from our screen, we determined that the initiation of BIR involves the histone methyltransferase Dot1 as well as Doa1, a protein involved in ubiquitination-mediated proteolysis. Deletion of the corresponding genes significantly impaired BIR in the ectopic (AM3422) (Fig. 6a and Supplementary Data 2) and allelic systems (Fig. 6b, c) and caused a synthesis defect during BIR initiation, as detected by AMBER (Fig. 6d, e, h). During later steps of BIR synthesis, we observed that two different Rpd3 deacetylase complexes—small-Rpd3S and large-Rpd3L (see in ref. 58)—have opposing roles in BIR. In particular, Rpd3L was determined to be important for BIR completion, while Rpd3S, which shares several common subunits with Rpd3L, was observed to inhibit BIR. These conclusions were supported by our finding that deleting RPD3 or UME1 (encoding common subunits of the Rpd3L and Rpd3S complexes) as well as CTI6 or SAP30 (specific to Rpd3L) reduced BIR efficiency (Fig. 6a), while deleting EAF3 (specific to Rpd3S) increased it (Fig. 6a). We further observed that the absence of Sdc1, which participates in histone 3 lysine 4 trimethylation (H3K4me3) 55 known to be involved in the recruitment of Rpd3L 59,60, decreased BIR efficiency (Supplementary Data 2). Finally, despite the significant defect in formation of BIR outcomes observed using genetic methods (Fig. 6c), BIR kinetics measured by AMBER in rpd3Δ and cti6Δ mutants was similar to WT (Fig. 6f–h). We therefore propose that Rpd3L is involved in the formation/stabilization of the final BIR product.

Further, discovering Eaf1—a component of the NuA4 histone acetyltransferase (HAT) complex 61—in our screen uncovered an important role for the NuA4-SWI/SNF axis in BIR. We specifically observed that deleting EAF1 caused a significant BIR defect in the ectopic system (AM3422; Fig. 6a). It is known that NuA4 recruits the SWI/SNF complex to DSBs 62, and, consistently, deletion of SNF6 and SNF12, which were identified in our screen, also caused a BIR defect (Fig. 6a). Interestingly, not every subunit of the NuA4 HAT complex played the same role in BIR. For instance, deleting EAF5 did not impact BIR (Supplementary Data 2), while deleting YAF9 increased BIR efficiency (Fig. 6a). Because Yaf9 is also a member of the SWR1 complex, we hypothesized that the yaf9Δ phenotype may be driven by its role in the SWR1 complex. Consistent with this idea, deleting HTZ1, which encodes histone variant H2A.Z deposited around DSBs by the SWR1 complex 63, mimicked the yaf9Δ phenotype, with htz1Δ cells showing increased BIR efficiency (Fig. 6a), tentatively suggesting that, at least within this experimental system, SWR1 may suppress BIR by promoting histone H2A.Z deposition after a DSB.

Other pathways that participate in BIR
Our screen also identified BIR candidate genes belonging to several other functional groups (Supplementary Fig. 7b and Supplementary Data 3). We observed that deletions of several genes involved in protein sorting and trafficking complexes impaired BIR. Also, deletions of the following genes involved in the cellular stress response significantly negatively affected BIR efficiency: SOK2, SLG1, SLT2, PHO85. Similarly, a significant reduction in BIR efficiency was observed following the deletion of MMS19, which encodes an iron-sulfur cluster assembly protein and was previously shown to affect fragility associated with inverted DNA repeats 64. Further functional characterization of these genes and their related protein complexes is needed to delineate their precise roles in BIR.
paper_content.methods:
Strains
Three experimental systems were used in this study to investigate BIR (see Supplementary Data 1): two haploid BIR systems—one based on yeast strain AM3422 and the other on strain YSJ131 45—where BIR proceeds through an ectopic position, and a disomic Chr III system (AM1411) in which DSBs are repaired by allelic BIR. We also used a YSJ133 45 which is isogenic to YSJ131 strain to conduct GC assay (see Supplementary Fig. 3a for details). AM1411 is a derivative of our BIR experimental strain, AM1003, which contains a truncated copy of Chr III that can be cut by a galactose-induced HO endonuclease at MATa and a full copy of Chr III that cannot be cut, as its Yα at MAT locus was deleted by the insertion of lys2-A7. AM1411 has the following genotype: MATa-LEU2-tel/MAT::lys2:A ade1 met13 ura3 leu2-3,112/leu2 thr4 hmlΔ::ADE1/hmlΔ::ADE3 hmrΔ::HPH ade3::GAL-HO FS2Δ::NAT/FS2 lys2Δ.

AM3422 is a new haploid BIR system, a derivative of KT556, which has the following genotype: MATa bar1Δ his7-2 trp1Δ ura3Δ leu2-3,112 ade2Δ lys2Δ cup1Δ yhr054cΔ cup2Δ V29616::CUP1 V34205::ADE2-HOcs-lys2Δ3’. This strain contains the ADE2 gene and a 5′ portion of LYS2 on Chr V between CAN1 and NPR2 genes. Importantly, there are no essential genes located centromere distal to this locus. The 3′ part of LYS2 is replaced with a modified version of the 117-bp HO endonuclease recognition cut site (see Supplementary Data 5 for the full sequence). This sequence allowed an efficient cutting (Supplementary Fig. 8), thereby promoting efficient BIR (Fig. 1b), but also allowed an optimal number of Lys+ papillae in a semi-quantitative BIR test (Fig. 1c), with no prior accumulation of Lys+. The 3′ part of the LYS2 gene (3812 bp) marked by TRP1 gene was inserted into HIS4 (position 65,934 to 68,333 bp of Chr III according to SGD). The two fragments of LYS2 (located on Chr V and Chr III) share 2339 bp of homology. Finally, the strain contains GAL::HO inserted into the ADE3 gene, while the HO gene at its native locus is deleted.

To construct the AM3874 strain used for the genome-wide screen for BIR regulators, the following modifications were made to AM3422. A NATMX cassette was inserted into the HIS4 locus 160 bp centromere distal to the lys2 fragment. The LEU2 gene at its native position in Chr III was replaced by URA3, and LEU2 was inserted into the AVT2 gene next to CAN1 to mark the 5′ part of lys2 on Chr V. Also, his7-2 was replaced by the wild type HIS7. The HIS4 gene was inserted into the native LYS2 locus on Chr II. This allowed for selection against the LYS2 allele of the YKO strains by selecting for His+. In addition, HIS3 was deleted at its native location by the delitto perfetto approach 81, while MFA1 was replaced by MFA-HIS3 (similar to refs. 64,82). We introduced a fragment containing the rpl28Q38K mutation (similar to refs. 64,82) by transformation using selection for resistance to cycloheximide. Finally, URA3 inserted at LEU2 was fully deleted while the URA3 gene was inserted next to (858 bp from) the ade3::GAL::HO cassette on Chr VII.

All single-gene deletion mutants were constructed by transformation with a PCR-derived KANMX, NATMX, HPHMX, or BleoR module, each flanked by sequences homologous to the regions surrounding the open reading frame of each gene 83,84. All constructs were confirmed by PCR and by phenotype. The bub1Δ, bub3Δ, mad2Δ, bub2Δ, bfa1Δ, and nup188Δ mutants were also tested by droplet digital (dd) PCR for the correct number of each chromosome, to make sure that these mutants were not aneuploids. See Supplementary Data 1 for the genotypes of all strains used in this study.

The strains used for ChIP analysis were generated by inserting a 13xMyc epitope tag, marked by KANMX at the C-terminus of the NUP84 and NUP188 coding sequences in the allelic BIR strain (Supplementary Data 1). The derivative strains were analyzed by BIR assay to confirm that the insertion of Myc tag did not affect the functions of Nup84 and Nup188 proteins (see Supplementary Data 4).

Media and growth conditions
Rich media, Yeast extract-peptone-dextrose (YEPD), YEP-Raffinose (YEP-Raf), YEP-Galactose (YEP-Gal), and YEP-Lactate (YEP-Lac) media were prepared as described 85. Antibiotics, including hygromycin, nourseothricin, G418, have been added to YEPD as described 85. Synthetic complete media with bases and amino acids omitted (SC-Leu, SC-Ura, SC-Ade, etc) were prepared as described 85. Sporulation medium with potassium acetate (KAC) was prepared as: 2% potassium acetate, 2.5% Agar, pH = 7. All yeast cultures were grown at 30°C.

BIR efficiency assay in the yeast ectopic systems
Cells of yeast strains including AM3422, YSJ131 and their derivatives were cultured in 2 ml YEP-Lac liquid media with aeration for 18–24 h until reaching a concentration of ~2×107 cells/mL. Next, the cultures were diluted and plated on YEPD and YEP-Gal media, at ~200 cells/plate. The colonies were counted after 3–4 days of incubation and the viability following the DSB was calculated as a ratio of the colony forming units (cfu) on YEP-Gal to YEPD. The difference in viability after DSB in mutant strains and WT was compared by one-way ANOVA (Supplementary Data 2). To determine the fraction of BIR repair among DSB repair outcomes, the colonies obtained from AM3422 and its derivatives grown on YEP-Gal (and YEPD as a control) were replica plated to SC-Ade and SC-Lys plates. The fraction of BIR was calculated as the fraction of Ade+ Lys-.

The chromosome structure of BIR repair outcomes was confirmed by CHEF gel electrophoresis followed by Southern blot analysis using CHEF-DRII (Bio-Rad) apparatus. The preparation of DNA for CHEF in agarose plugs was performed as previously described in ref. 85. The running conditions for CHEF were optimized for the maximal separation of Chr V and Chr III, as follows: initial switch time of 35.43 s, final switch time of 52.33 s, running time of 39 h, and voltage of 6 Volts/cm. Following separating by CHEF, the DSB repair products were hybridized to P32-labeled probes specific to MGR1 (on the left arm of Chr III) and to GLN3 (on the right arm of Chr V) (see Supplementary Data 5 for the sequences of oligonucleotides used to create probes). Prior to BIR, the MGR1 (Chr III)-specific probe detected a 337 kb-long Chr III. After BIR, the MGR1 probe detected both the original Chr III and a Chr V/Chr III recombinant chromosome, which was 619 kb in size. The latter product was also hybridized to the GLN3 (Chr V) specific probe.

BIR assay in the yeast allelic (disomic chromosome III) system
Cells of yeast strain AM1411 and its derivatives were cultured in YEP-Lac liquid medium, diluted and plated on YEPD and YEP-Gal plates at ~50–100 cells per plate, and viability following the DSB was calculated as a ratio of cfu on YEP-Gal to YEPD. Colonies grown on YEP-Gal (and on YEPD as a control) were replica-pated onto SC-Leu, SC-Ade, and based on the phenotype were classified as follows: Leu+ Ade+ as GC, Leu- Ade+ as BIR or BIR associated with GCR, Leu- Ade- white as HC, and Leu- Ade- red as CL. The full analysis of DSB repair outcomes is presented in Supplementary Data 4. To distinguish BIR from GCR outcomes, DNA purified from Leu- Ade+ repair outcomes was analyzed by CHEF, with initial switch time of 10 s, final switch time of 35 s, running time of 40 h, and voltage of 6 Volts/cm, similar to 85.

Kinetics of BIR synthesis
The kinetics of BIR synthesis was analyzed using our recently developed ddPCR-based method called Assay for Monitoring BIR Elongation Rate (AMBER) 49. Yeast cells were cultured overnight in 5 ml SC-Leu medium, then transferred to YEP medium containing 2% raffinose and incubated for approximately 16 h, until the cell density reached ~5×106 cells per ml. A 10 ml aliquot was collected for analysis of pre-DSB copy number (“0h”), and 2% galactose was added to the remaining culture to induce DSB formation. Samples (10 ml each) were taken every 2 h for up to 10 h. Cells were resuspended in spheroplasting buffer (0.4 M sorbitol, 0.4 M KCl, 40 mM sodium phosphate buffer [pH 7.2], 0.5 mM MgCl2) containing 20T zymolyase (250 µg per ml) and incubated at 37°C for 10 min to digest the cell wall. Approximately 2.5×105 cells were then centrifuged at 1000×g for 2 min, and the supernatant was discarded. The pellet was resuspended in 400 µl of 1× NEB rCutSmart buffer (B6004S). Next, 4 µl of 10% SDS was added, and the mixture was incubated at 60°C for 15 min. The sample was cooled on ice, followed by addition of 50 µl 10% Triton X-100. RNase A (20 µl, 10 mg per ml) was then added, and the mixture was incubated at 37°C for 30 min. Subsequently, 20 µl protease K (10 mg per ml) was added and incubated at 60°C for 30 min. After cooling on ice for 5 min, 0.5 ml of phenol–chloroform was added, and the mixture was centrifuged at 16,000×g for 15 min. The aqueous phase was extracted with an additional 0.5 ml of phenol–chloroform, mixed by inversion, and centrifuged. DNA was precipitated from the final aqueous phase by adding 35 µl of 3 M Sodium acetate [pH 5.2] and 0.35 ml of isopropanol, followed by incubation at room temperature for 30 min. DNA was pelleted by centrifugation at 16,000×g for 20 min, and the supernatant was removed. The pellet was washed with 0.5 ml 80% ethanol, centrifuged at 16,000×g for 5 min, and air-dried. The dried DNA pellet was resuspended in 100 µl of molecular-grade water for subsequent analysis. Purified DNA was quantified by ddPCR using standard reaction conditions. BIR synthesis was followed by tracking the copy number increase along the track of BIR normalized to copy number at ACT1 located on Chr VI, using QX600 ddPCR software, similarly to ref. 49. See Supplementary Data 5 for the sequences of oligos used for this assay. Also, see Supplementary Data 6 for AMBER data obtained in each individual experiment.

Genome-wide screen for BIR genes
The screen was performed by the following steps:
1. AM3874 (Supplementary Data 1) cells were cultured in 500 ml liquid YEPD medium for 24 h. Concomitantly, the cells from the MATα YKO yeast collection (horizondiscovery.com/en/non-mammalian-research-tools/products/yeast-knockout), which represents a collection of approximately 5000 strains with deletions of individual non-essential genes in the BY4742 strain with the genotype MATα his3Δ-1 leu2Δ0 lys2Δ0 ura3Δ0 were grown overnight in 96-well plates with 100 µL of liquid YEPD medium per well.
2. 100 µl of AM3874 culture was added to each well of the 96-well plates for mating with the individual gene deletion strains. The strain mixtures were incubated overnight to allow efficient strain hybridization.
3. To select for the resulting hybrids (diploids), 10 µl of each mixture was placed on YEPD plates containing G418 (0.5 g per liter) and nourseothricin (0.1 g per liter), followed by overnight incubation.
4. Plates from Step 3 were replica plated onto sporulation (Kac) medium and incubated for 72 h at 30°C.
5. The sporulating cultures were replica plated onto YEPD plates containing G418 (0.5 g per liter), nourseothricin (0.1 g per liter), and cycloheximide (0.01 g per liter) and incubated for 48 h at 30°C.
6. Plates were replica plated onto SC-(Leu, His, Ura) and incubated for 48 h at 30°C.
7. Plates were replica plated onto YEPD+G418, nourseothricin, and cycloheximide and incubated for 48 h at 30°C.
8. Plates were replica-plated to SC-Lys and incubated for 48 h at 30°C.
9. BIR-defective mutants were identified based on a reduced number of Lys+ papillae on the patch (semi-quantitative BIR efficiency assay) compared to WT.

Assessment of cell cycle progression by microscopic analysis
A BIR repair time-course experiment was conducted in derivatives of the AM1411 strain in YEP-Lac, similar to described in ref. 85. Fifty-ml cell samples were collected before and at time points following DSB induction (galactose addition) for 12 h. To fix live cells, a spun-down pellet was resuspended in 500 μL of water, which was then thoroughly mixed with 500 μL of 100% ethanol. The mixture was stored at 4°C until the entire time-course experiment was completed. Fixed cells were twice washed with sterile water. Prior to imaging, 20–50 μL of the mixture was aliquoted in a new microcentrifuge tube and spun down at 800×g for 1 min, and the supernatant was completely removed. The pellet was then resuspended in 12 μL SlowFade TM DAPI (Thermo Fisher #S36964) and used to prepare microscope slides. Images were taken using Leica Widefield fluorescence microscope with a 40× magnification lens and acquired using LASX software.

ChIP assay
Yeast cells were cultured in YEP-raffinose liquid medium overnight at 30°C to achieve a density of 1×107 cells/mL before adding galactose (2% final concentration) to introduce DSB. Cells were fixed in formaldehyde (1% final concentration) to cross-link DNA–protein complexes. After 10 min, the cross-linking reactions were quenched by the addition of glycine (125 mM), and the reaction continued for 5 min on a shaker. The cells were collected by centrifugation and washed first with TBS (125 mM Tris-HCl [pH 7.4], 130 mM NaCl, 5 mM KCl, 0.9 mM CaCl2, and 0.5 mM MgCl2) supplemented with glycine (125 mM), followed by a second wash in TBS alone. Cells were resuspended in lysis buffer (50 mM HEPES [pH 7.5], 1 mM EDTA, 140 mM NaCl, 1% Triton X-100, 0.1% sodium deoxycholate, 1 mg/mL bacitracin, 1 mM benzamidine, and 1 mM PMSF). Glass beads were added to the cells suspension, followed by cell disruption in a bead beater for 6 min (1 min disruption each time with 2 min on-ice intervals). The cell lysate containing the genomic DNA was sheared to fragments with an average size of 0.5 kb by sonication (Bioruptor® Pico Sonicator B01080010). The cell debris was sedimented by centrifugation at 16,000×g for 20 min, and the collected supernatant was distributed into IP (Input) and Non-IP (Non-Input). For the IP samples, incubation was performed overnight with anti-c-Myc antibody (Sigma M4439) or anti-Rad51 antibody (a gift from Dr. Patrick Sung) at 4°C, followed by the addition of Dynabeads Protein G (Thermo, 1004D) and continued incubation for 4 h. Beads were then washed twice with lysis buffer, twice with high-salt lysis buffer (lysis buffer with 500 mM NaCl), twice with wash buffer (10 mM Tris-HCl [pH 8.0], 1 mM EDTA, 250 mM LiCl, 0.5% sodium deoxycholate, and 0.5% Igepal CA-630), and twice with 1× TE. DNA–protein complexes were eluted by incubating beads with 100 μL of elution buffer (50 mM Tris-HCl [pH 8.0], 10 mM EDTA, and 1% SDS) for 30 min at 65°C. Reverse cross-linking was carried out overnight at 65°C, followed by proteinase K treatment and phenol–chloroform purification of DNA. Purified DNA was analyzed by qPCR using the PowerUp SYBR Green Master Mix (Applied Biosystems, 4367659). Enrichment was normalized to the ACT1 locus. Accumulation of targeted proteins after DSB measured by ChIP is calculated by subtraction from before DSB.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
Liu et al. conducted a genome-wide screen to identify new break-induced replication (BIR) genes in yeast using an ectopic BIR assay with non-essential gene knockouts (KOs). This screen uncovered 37 novel BIR genes involved in various biological processes, including the spindle assembly checkpoint (SAC), the spindle position checkpoint (SPOC), nuclear pore/migration, and chromatin and post-translational modifications.
The study employs multiple assays, including another BIR assay (disomic assay) and the AMBER assay, to further validate and analyze the potential roles of SAC and SPOC in BIR. The authors also discuss the possible influence of epigenetic modifications of chromatin and nuclear pore components; however, these sections lack a clear mechanistic explanation, making them feel incomplete. It is somewhat surprising that so many pathways are interconnected with BIR, and many likely influence BIR indirectly by broadly regulating the cell cycle and stress responses. Nonetheless, the study is rigorous, employing multiple validation assays, and provides an initial framework for further exploration of this critical process in both yeast and human cells.
Key Questions and Considerations:
1. Can we test whether the prolonged duration of the current BIR system is responsible for its dependence on SAC? If we analyze BIR systems that require shorter DNA synthesis, as described by Symington or Haber, would BIR still be dependent on SAC or SPOC?
2. Can we distinguish whether the authors observed low cell viability or simply a prolonged cell cycle delay due to extended BIR in SPOC mutants?
3. Is the lethality of nup188 not offset by mad2 deletion because it may also be involved in the DNA damage response (DDR)? Is deletion of RAD9 partially rescue the low viability in nup188?
4. The discrepancy between BIR defects in mad2 using the disomic versus ectopic reporters is puzzling. The authors should resolve this inconsistency and ensure that candidate mutants showing BIR defects are consistently identified, regardless of the strain used to study BIR function.
5. Why is half crossover (HC) formation reduced in bub3 mutants?
6. The selection of 92 genes out of approximately 300 based solely on known gene function seems arbitrary. What criteria were used for this selection? The full list should be provided in the supplementary data.
7. Besides EAF3, did the screen identify any other genes that enhance BIR?
8. I noticed that HC formation is significantly increased in mad2 mutants. Can HC still generate Lys+ colonies in the ectopic assay?
9. In bub2 mutants, HC is not detected. What could be the underlying reason?
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
Hiu et al. conducted a genetic screen focused on non-essential genes in budding yeast to identify factors mediating break-induced replication (BIR), a DNA repair pathway that can drive chromosome instability and contribute to tumorigenesis in mammals. The results present a list of 37 genes as novel candidate regulators of BIR-mediated repair. Most of the gene hits are known to be associated with or linked to diverse molecular pathways. The authors assessed the impact of many of these hits in various versions of BIR reporter assays, which included different genetic reporter assays and copy-number assessments targeting chromosomal regions proximal or distal to the DNA break site (serving as a readout of early vs. late BIR; or BIR initiation vs. BIR progression). Experiments involved evaluating the usage of BIR compared to other potential options (e.g., GC, HC, or CL), cell cycle progression, and cell viability. Overall, the authors draw several main conclusions: the Spindle Assembly Checkpoint (SAC) is required for BIR, the Spindle Position Checkpoint (SPOC) is necessary for BIR, Nuclear pore proteins (Nup84 vs. Nup188) have multiple roles in BIR, and various post-translational modifications are important for successful BIR repair.
Overall, the genetic screening conducted will interest researchers across various fields, including yeast genetics, checkpoint signaling, and genome stability. The authors deserve commendation for utilizing and clearly explaining several sophisticated genetic assays to evaluate BIR within different chromosomal contexts. However, this reviewer has several significant concerns that prevent the publication of this manuscript in its current form.
Major concerns:
The study is too preliminary and underdeveloped. In its present form, it may be better suited for a journal that reports genetic screen results without a significant level of mechanistic understanding or conceptual advance. However, as outlined below, these weaknesses may be addressable through a major revision.
Many unsubstantiated assumptions and speculations are made, leaving the data insufficient to support the claims. A significant weakness of the study is the interpretation of weak correlations as causations. The authors often conflate the effect of knocking out individual genes with the disruption of the known pathway where the gene product typically operates, and no robust experiments or controls are executed to establish strong causal relationships between the allegedly impacted pathway and the observed decrease in BIR.
Additionally, within each pathway claimed to be required for efficient BIR, how many non-essential genes exist in yeast, how many of those genes were identified as hits in the genetic screen, and how many have been evaluated in post-screen BIR validation assays? In other words, what percentage of non-essential genes linked to SAC, SPOC, NPCs, etc., are required for efficient BIR? Is the relationship between each of these sets of genes epistatic (e.g., BUB1, BUB3, and MAD2; Nup84 and Nup188; etc.) in terms of their effect on BIR?
How do the authors rule out the possibility that the proposed genes may impact BIR by operating independently of their known functions, such as through moonlighting-type roles? Similarly, additional molecular or cellular biological mechanistic insight would be beneficial. For instance, what is the exact molecular relationship between factors that regulate the proper attachment of microtubules to the kinetochore during mitosis and the supposedly prolonged G2/M arrest required for BIR repair? Which molecular steps of BIR-based repair rely on Nup84 versus Nup188, and why? How does this explain the apparent dependence on Nup84 for BIR initiation and on Nup188 for BIR completion? Overall, the authors could focus on providing further mechanistic insights related to a few of their numerous major claims to offer more robust support while possibly toning down other claims that lack detailed mechanistic/experimental insight.
Statistical analyses were often not depicted in the graphs (e.g., Fig. 1b, 2a,e-h, 3c-k, 4a-c,f-g, 5a-b,g-j, 6a,d-h) or may have been inappropriate. For instance, the supplemental table with the original results of the BIR screen (Supp Table 2) includes a t-test comparing all mutants to the WT. Since all mutants are compared to the same WT condition, the t-test is likely inappropriate and should be replaced with an ANOVA using multiple comparisons or a similar test that adjusts for multiple comparisons. Whether and how correcting the statistical analyses would change the list of screen hits identified and the overall results is a significant question. Additionally, the statistical analyses presented were sometimes unclear; for example, in Fig. 2d, was a Bonferroni correction or a similar adjustment applied for the multiple comparisons involving the WT condition?
Caution is advised when interpreting the knockout of a specific gene that affects BIR in only some of the BIR assays utilized. How might the specific chromosomal context of the reporter DSB assay influence the interpretation of these results?
Other point(s):
Although the text is well-written, a more thorough proofreading or professional English editing would significantly enhance the manuscript. A particularly frequent mistake was concerning the use of the definite article "the."
Given the important concerns outlined above, the manuscript's title and abstract could be misleading and should be revised with care.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
The manuscript by Liu, Lee et al represents a highly valuable addition to the understanding of the BIR process, a very important sub-pathway of homology-mediated repair of broken chromosomes. Defects in this process lead to the formation of structural genomic variants that are directly implicated in many disease processes. As noted by the authors, the number of cellular factors known to be involved in BIR is relatively limited, especially due to the lack of systematic efforts to identify them. This study is highly innovative in at least two ways. First, it reports on the results of such a systematic screen and uncovers dozens of new BIR factors, opening multiple exciting opportunities for follow-up research. Second, the authors present a comprehensive characterization of some of the most intriguing hits from their screen, in particular the genes involved in late cell cycle checkpoints (SAC and SPOC). The latter is very helpful in clarifying the relationship between the slow kinetics of BIR repair, and the need for fast-dividing cells to delay mitosis until BIR is completed. The authors also provide initial investigations of hits associated with the nuclear pore complex and chromatin structure, although not quite as in depth. Until now, studies of the BIR mechanism mostly focused on factors directly involved in DNA metabolism and repair (eg Pol32, Pif1, Rad51). Following this study, the range of cellular functions that will be investigated is expected to expand greatly, thus representing an influential contribution to the field.
Below are relatively minor comments, curiosities, suggestions that the authors and editors might wish to consider in a revised manuscript.
-The authors did a genomic (CHEF) analysis (Fig. 5) of the Leu- Ade+ clones derived from the nup mutants and showed that some of them were not regular BIR, but instead contained some GCRs. That analysis was quite informative, thus raising the question: Was this type of genomic analysis also done for the bub mutants (Fig. 2,3,4)? If not, should it be done? Given that the SAC and SPOC pathways were the major focus of the work following the screening phase, I think it might be important to add some information about this. In other words, how sure are the authors that Leu- Ade+ clones derived mutants such as bub2D or bfa1D actually mostly carry BIR products?
-Another aspect that I think should be commented on is the remarkable absence of half-crossovers (HC) in bub2D and nup184D. Both of these mutants displayed a massive drop in viability following DSB induction, and in both HCs were almost entirely gone. Is there a relationship? The authors included some discussion about gene conversions (GC), pointing out that GCs are in a “fast” repair class of products. HCs might also be in that “fast” repair group, so why are HCs gone while GCs increase (in bub2D)? I think this warrants some discussion.
-Finally, and not as relevant, I was a bit intrigued by the meaning of flower and bee in Figure 1e. I am not against it, but I did not find any comment in the manuscript or the figure legend to explain its meaning. I suggest the authors add some comment to provide context to the readers about why the diagram was drawn as such.

Response to reviewer’s comments:
Reviewer #1
Reviewer 1, Comment 1. Liu et al. conducted a genome-wide screen to identify new
break-induced replication (BIR) genes in yeast using an ectopic BIR assay with non-
essential gene knockouts (KOs). This screen uncovered 37 novel BIR genes involved in
various biological processes, including the spindle assembly checkpoint (SAC), the
spindle position checkpoint (SPOC), nuclear pore/migration, and chromatin and post-
translational modifications.
The study employs multiple assays, including another BIR assay (disomic assay) and
the AMBER assay, to further validate and analyze the potential roles of SAC and SPOC
in BIR. The authors also discuss the possible influence of epigenetic modifications of
chromatin and nuclear pore components; however, these sections lack a clear
mechanistic explanation, making them feel incomplete. It is somewhat surprising that so
many pathways are interconnected with BIR, and many likely influence BIR indirectly by
broadly regulating the cell cycle and stress responses. Nonetheless, the study is
rigorous, employing multiple validation assays, and provides an initial framework for
further exploration of this critical process in both yeast and human cells.
Reviewer 1, Response 1. We thank the Reviewer for these comments. Indeed, our
goal was to create a complete list of non-essential yeast genes that are required for
BIR. As the Reviewer notes, this effort yielded a long list of genes across many
pathways, which made it impossible for us to complete mechanistic analyses for every
gene/pathway. Instead, we decided to prioritize depth over breadth regarding
mechanistic studies, selecting only a few pathways for characterization. In our revised
manuscript, we maintained our focus on these selected pathways, but we have
significantly expanded the amount of mechanistic detail regarding their involvement in
BIR.
Reviewer 1, Comment 2. Can we test whether the prolonged duration of the current
BIR system is responsible for its dependence on SAC? If we analyze BIR systems that
require shorter DNA synthesis, as described by Symington or Haber, would BIR still be
dependent on SAC or SPOC?
Reviewer 1, Response 2. In response to this comment, we followed the Reviewer’s
suggestion and studied the dependence of SAC and SPOC genes in a yeast
experimental BIR system that requires shorter DNA synthesis, as published in (JAIN et
al. 2009). DSBs in this system are induced at Chr V, and the centromere-proximal end
invades into Chr III to complete BIR repair by synthesizing 41 kb of DNA (Fig. 2b;
Supplementary Fig. 3a, b; Supplementary Table 2.2). In this system (YSJ131), both
mad2Δ (SAC) and bub2Δ (SPOC) significantly reduced BIR efficiency, which led to
significantly reduced cell viability following DSB induction compared to wild type cells
(Fig. 2b, Supplementary Fig. 3b). Therefore, this represents the third system in which
we demonstrate the dependence of BIR on the SAC and SPOC. However, to the
Reviewer’s point, we cannot fully exclude that this dependence could be decreased or
eliminated in some other exceptionally fast and efficient BIR systems.

suitable homologous sequence and to subsequently synthesize DNA. This notion is
supported by our finding that mad2Δ and bub2Δ were defective in gene conversion
(GC) requiring 5 kb of DNA repair synthesis in an isogenic to YSJ131, system (YSJ133)
(JAIN et al. 2009), in which the DSB is induced at the same location as in this new
ectopic BIR system (YSJ131) (Supplementary Fig. 3a, b); however, mad2Δ and bub2Δ
were as proficient as WT at completing GC with copying ~5 kb in our allelic disomic
system in which the homology search between allelic locations is much faster (Fig. 2d,
Fig. 4d). The new data were added to Fig. 2b and to the Supplementary Fig. 3a-b, with
all raw data included in Supplementary Tables 2.2 and 2.3. Also, we added the following
sentences to the Results section:
• In support of this hypothesis, we observed a defective BIR in bub1Δ, bub3Δ, and
mad2Δ mutants in two ectopic BIR systems (AM3422 and YSJ131; Fig. 2 a, b;
Supplementary Fig. 3a, b, Supplementary Tables 2.1 and 2.2).
“However, in an ectopic system (YSJ133), where the homology search takes
longer and even GC can triggers checkpoint arrest BUB2 deletion led to a
modest decrease in GC efficiency (Supplementary Fig. 3b), but the defect of BIR
in this system (YSJ131) was more severe (Supplementary Fig. 3b).”
Reviewer 1, Comment 3. Can we distinguish whether the authors observed low cell
viability or simply a prolonged cell cycle delay due to extended BIR in SPOC mutants?
Reviewer 1, Response 3. To address this concern, we plated bfa1Δ and bub2Δ cells
on YEPD and YEP-Gal media and incubated the plates at 30 οC for 10 days. Cell
viability was calculated as the number of colonies formed on YEP-Gal over the number
of colonies formed on YEPD. Viability in bfa1Δ and bub2Δ cells after 10 days was low
and similar to viability previously observed after 5 days of growth. Importantly,
microscopic examination demonstrated that, among the cells that did not form colonies,
81% of bfa1Δ (34/42) and 47% of bub2Δ (26/55) cells stayed below the 4-cell stage.
Among the other plated cells that didn’t form colony, most divided fewer than 3 times,
and all of them contained fewer than 14 cells. Our results indicate that the low colony-
forming efficiency we observed following DSB induction in SPOC mutants results from
cell death rather than from slow growth associated with a prolonged cell cycle delay.
These data were added to Supplemental Fig. 3d, and the following sentence was added
to the Results section:

medium, most bub2Δ cells divided no more than twice, and no cells formed
micro-colonies after DSB induction (Supplementary Fig. 3d) confirming lethality
following the DSB.”
Reviewer 1, Comment 4. Is the lethality of nup188 not offset by mad2 deletion
because it may also be involved in the DNA damage response (DDR)? Is deletion of
RAD9 partially rescue the low viability in nup188?
