## Methods

Strains
Three experimental systems were used in this study to investigate BIR (see Supplementary Data 1): two haploid BIR systems—one based on yeast strain AM3422 and the other on strain YSJ131 45—where BIR proceeds through an ectopic position, and a disomic Chr III system (AM1411) in which DSBs are repaired by allelic BIR. We also used a YSJ133 45 which is isogenic to YSJ131 strain to conduct GC assay (see Supplementary Fig. 3a for details). AM1411 is a derivative of our BIR experimental strain, AM1003, which contains a truncated copy of Chr III that can be cut by a galactose-induced HO endonuclease at MATa and a full copy of Chr III that cannot be cut, as its Yα at MAT locus was deleted by the insertion of lys2-A7. AM1411 has the following genotype: MATa-LEU2-tel/MAT::lys2:A ade1 met13 ura3 leu2-3,112/leu2 thr4 hmlΔ::ADE1/hmlΔ::ADE3 hmrΔ::HPH ade3::GAL-HO FS2Δ::NAT/FS2 lys2Δ.

AM3422 is a new haploid BIR system, a derivative of KT556, which has the following genotype: MATa bar1Δ his7-2 trp1Δ ura3Δ leu2-3,112 ade2Δ lys2Δ cup1Δ yhr054cΔ cup2Δ V29616::CUP1 V34205::ADE2-HOcs-lys2Δ3’. This strain contains the ADE2 gene and a 5′ portion of LYS2 on Chr V between CAN1 and NPR2 genes. Importantly, there are no essential genes located centromere distal to this locus. The 3′ part of LYS2 is replaced with a modified version of the 117-bp HO endonuclease recognition cut site (see Supplementary Data 5 for the full sequence). This sequence allowed an efficient cutting (Supplementary Fig. 8), thereby promoting efficient BIR (Fig. 1b), but also allowed an optimal number of Lys+ papillae in a semi-quantitative BIR test (Fig. 1c), with no prior accumulation of Lys+. The 3′ part of the LYS2 gene (3812 bp) marked by TRP1 gene was inserted into HIS4 (position 65,934 to 68,333 bp of Chr III according to SGD). The two fragments of LYS2 (located on Chr V and Chr III) share 2339 bp of homology. Finally, the strain contains GAL::HO inserted into the ADE3 gene, while the HO gene at its native locus is deleted.

To construct the AM3874 strain used for the genome-wide screen for BIR regulators, the following modifications were made to AM3422. A NATMX cassette was inserted into the HIS4 locus 160 bp centromere distal to the lys2 fragment. The LEU2 gene at its native position in Chr III was replaced by URA3, and LEU2 was inserted into the AVT2 gene next to CAN1 to mark the 5′ part of lys2 on Chr V. Also, his7-2 was replaced by the wild type HIS7. The HIS4 gene was inserted into the native LYS2 locus on Chr II. This allowed for selection against the LYS2 allele of the YKO strains by selecting for His+. In addition, HIS3 was deleted at its native location by the delitto perfetto approach 81, while MFA1 was replaced by MFA-HIS3 (similar to refs. 64,82). We introduced a fragment containing the rpl28Q38K mutation (similar to refs. 64,82) by transformation using selection for resistance to cycloheximide. Finally, URA3 inserted at LEU2 was fully deleted while the URA3 gene was inserted next to (858 bp from) the ade3::GAL::HO cassette on Chr VII.

All single-gene deletion mutants were constructed by transformation with a PCR-derived KANMX, NATMX, HPHMX, or BleoR module, each flanked by sequences homologous to the regions surrounding the open reading frame of each gene 83,84. All constructs were confirmed by PCR and by phenotype. The bub1Δ, bub3Δ, mad2Δ, bub2Δ, bfa1Δ, and nup188Δ mutants were also tested by droplet digital (dd) PCR for the correct number of each chromosome, to make sure that these mutants were not aneuploids. See Supplementary Data 1 for the genotypes of all strains used in this study.

The strains used for ChIP analysis were generated by inserting a 13xMyc epitope tag, marked by KANMX at the C-terminus of the NUP84 and NUP188 coding sequences in the allelic BIR strain (Supplementary Data 1). The derivative strains were analyzed by BIR assay to confirm that the insertion of Myc tag did not affect the functions of Nup84 and Nup188 proteins (see Supplementary Data 4).

Media and growth conditions
Rich media, Yeast extract-peptone-dextrose (YEPD), YEP-Raffinose (YEP-Raf), YEP-Galactose (YEP-Gal), and YEP-Lactate (YEP-Lac) media were prepared as described 85. Antibiotics, including hygromycin, nourseothricin, G418, have been added to YEPD as described 85. Synthetic complete media with bases and amino acids omitted (SC-Leu, SC-Ura, SC-Ade, etc) were prepared as described 85. Sporulation medium with potassium acetate (KAC) was prepared as: 2% potassium acetate, 2.5% Agar, pH = 7. All yeast cultures were grown at 30°C.

BIR efficiency assay in the yeast ectopic systems
Cells of yeast strains including AM3422, YSJ131 and their derivatives were cultured in 2 ml YEP-Lac liquid media with aeration for 18–24 h until reaching a concentration of ~2×107 cells/mL. Next, the cultures were diluted and plated on YEPD and YEP-Gal media, at ~200 cells/plate. The colonies were counted after 3–4 days of incubation and the viability following the DSB was calculated as a ratio of the colony forming units (cfu) on YEP-Gal to YEPD. The difference in viability after DSB in mutant strains and WT was compared by one-way ANOVA (Supplementary Data 2). To determine the fraction of BIR repair among DSB repair outcomes, the colonies obtained from AM3422 and its derivatives grown on YEP-Gal (and YEPD as a control) were replica plated to SC-Ade and SC-Lys plates. The fraction of BIR was calculated as the fraction of Ade+ Lys-.

The chromosome structure of BIR repair outcomes was confirmed by CHEF gel electrophoresis followed by Southern blot analysis using CHEF-DRII (Bio-Rad) apparatus. The preparation of DNA for CHEF in agarose plugs was performed as previously described in ref. 85. The running conditions for CHEF were optimized for the maximal separation of Chr V and Chr III, as follows: initial switch time of 35.43 s, final switch time of 52.33 s, running time of 39 h, and voltage of 6 Volts/cm. Following separating by CHEF, the DSB repair products were hybridized to P32-labeled probes specific to MGR1 (on the left arm of Chr III) and to GLN3 (on the right arm of Chr V) (see Supplementary Data 5 for the sequences of oligonucleotides used to create probes). Prior to BIR, the MGR1 (Chr III)-specific probe detected a 337 kb-long Chr III. After BIR, the MGR1 probe detected both the original Chr III and a Chr V/Chr III recombinant chromosome, which was 619 kb in size. The latter product was also hybridized to the GLN3 (Chr V) specific probe.

BIR assay in the yeast allelic (disomic chromosome III) system
Cells of yeast strain AM1411 and its derivatives were cultured in YEP-Lac liquid medium, diluted and plated on YEPD and YEP-Gal plates at ~50–100 cells per plate, and viability following the DSB was calculated as a ratio of cfu on YEP-Gal to YEPD. Colonies grown on YEP-Gal (and on YEPD as a control) were replica-pated onto SC-Leu, SC-Ade, and based on the phenotype were classified as follows: Leu+ Ade+ as GC, Leu- Ade+ as BIR or BIR associated with GCR, Leu- Ade- white as HC, and Leu- Ade- red as CL. The full analysis of DSB repair outcomes is presented in Supplementary Data 4. To distinguish BIR from GCR outcomes, DNA purified from Leu- Ade+ repair outcomes was analyzed by CHEF, with initial switch time of 10 s, final switch time of 35 s, running time of 40 h, and voltage of 6 Volts/cm, similar to 85.

Kinetics of BIR synthesis
The kinetics of BIR synthesis was analyzed using our recently developed ddPCR-based method called Assay for Monitoring BIR Elongation Rate (AMBER) 49. Yeast cells were cultured overnight in 5 ml SC-Leu medium, then transferred to YEP medium containing 2% raffinose and incubated for approximately 16 h, until the cell density reached ~5×106 cells per ml. A 10 ml aliquot was collected for analysis of pre-DSB copy number (“0h”), and 2% galactose was added to the remaining culture to induce DSB formation. Samples (10 ml each) were taken every 2 h for up to 10 h. Cells were resuspended in spheroplasting buffer (0.4 M sorbitol, 0.4 M KCl, 40 mM sodium phosphate buffer [pH 7.2], 0.5 mM MgCl2) containing 20T zymolyase (250 µg per ml) and incubated at 37°C for 10 min to digest the cell wall. Approximately 2.5×105 cells were then centrifuged at 1000×g for 2 min, and the supernatant was discarded. The pellet was resuspended in 400 µl of 1× NEB rCutSmart buffer (B6004S). Next, 4 µl of 10% SDS was added, and the mixture was incubated at 60°C for 15 min. The sample was cooled on ice, followed by addition of 50 µl 10% Triton X-100. RNase A (20 µl, 10 mg per ml) was then added, and the mixture was incubated at 37°C for 30 min. Subsequently, 20 µl protease K (10 mg per ml) was added and incubated at 60°C for 30 min. After cooling on ice for 5 min, 0.5 ml of phenol–chloroform was added, and the mixture was centrifuged at 16,000×g for 15 min. The aqueous phase was extracted with an additional 0.5 ml of phenol–chloroform, mixed by inversion, and centrifuged. DNA was precipitated from the final aqueous phase by adding 35 µl of 3 M Sodium acetate [pH 5.2] and 0.35 ml of isopropanol, followed by incubation at room temperature for 30 min. DNA was pelleted by centrifugation at 16,000×g for 20 min, and the supernatant was removed. The pellet was washed with 0.5 ml 80% ethanol, centrifuged at 16,000×g for 5 min, and air-dried. The dried DNA pellet was resuspended in 100 µl of molecular-grade water for subsequent analysis. Purified DNA was quantified by ddPCR using standard reaction conditions. BIR synthesis was followed by tracking the copy number increase along the track of BIR normalized to copy number at ACT1 located on Chr VI, using QX600 ddPCR software, similarly to ref. 49. See Supplementary Data 5 for the sequences of oligos used for this assay. Also, see Supplementary Data 6 for AMBER data obtained in each individual experiment.

Genome-wide screen for BIR genes
The screen was performed by the following steps:
1. AM3874 (Supplementary Data 1) cells were cultured in 500 ml liquid YEPD medium for 24 h. Concomitantly, the cells from the MATα YKO yeast collection (horizondiscovery.com/en/non-mammalian-research-tools/products/yeast-knockout), which represents a collection of approximately 5000 strains with deletions of individual non-essential genes in the BY4742 strain with the genotype MATα his3Δ-1 leu2Δ0 lys2Δ0 ura3Δ0 were grown overnight in 96-well plates with 100 µL of liquid YEPD medium per well.
2. 100 µl of AM3874 culture was added to each well of the 96-well plates for mating with the individual gene deletion strains. The strain mixtures were incubated overnight to allow efficient strain hybridization.
3. To select for the resulting hybrids (diploids), 10 µl of each mixture was placed on YEPD plates containing G418 (0.5 g per liter) and nourseothricin (0.1 g per liter), followed by overnight incubation.
4. Plates from Step 3 were replica plated onto sporulation (Kac) medium and incubated for 72 h at 30°C.
5. The sporulating cultures were replica plated onto YEPD plates containing G418 (0.5 g per liter), nourseothricin (0.1 g per liter), and cycloheximide (0.01 g per liter) and incubated for 48 h at 30°C.
6. Plates were replica plated onto SC-(Leu, His, Ura) and incubated for 48 h at 30°C.
7. Plates were replica plated onto YEPD+G418, nourseothricin, and cycloheximide and incubated for 48 h at 30°C.
8. Plates were replica-plated to SC-Lys and incubated for 48 h at 30°C.
9. BIR-defective mutants were identified based on a reduced number of Lys+ papillae on the patch (semi-quantitative BIR efficiency assay) compared to WT.

Assessment of cell cycle progression by microscopic analysis
A BIR repair time-course experiment was conducted in derivatives of the AM1411 strain in YEP-Lac, similar to described in ref. 85. Fifty-ml cell samples were collected before and at time points following DSB induction (galactose addition) for 12 h. To fix live cells, a spun-down pellet was resuspended in 500 μL of water, which was then thoroughly mixed with 500 μL of 100% ethanol. The mixture was stored at 4°C until the entire time-course experiment was completed. Fixed cells were twice washed with sterile water. Prior to imaging, 20–50 μL of the mixture was aliquoted in a new microcentrifuge tube and spun down at 800×g for 1 min, and the supernatant was completely removed. The pellet was then resuspended in 12 μL SlowFade TM DAPI (Thermo Fisher #S36964) and used to prepare microscope slides. Images were taken using Leica Widefield fluorescence microscope with a 40× magnification lens and acquired using LASX software.

ChIP assay
Yeast cells were cultured in YEP-raffinose liquid medium overnight at 30°C to achieve a density of 1×107 cells/mL before adding galactose (2% final concentration) to introduce DSB. Cells were fixed in formaldehyde (1% final concentration) to cross-link DNA–protein complexes. After 10 min, the cross-linking reactions were quenched by the addition of glycine (125 mM), and the reaction continued for 5 min on a shaker. The cells were collected by centrifugation and washed first with TBS (125 mM Tris-HCl [pH 7.4], 130 mM NaCl, 5 mM KCl, 0.9 mM CaCl2, and 0.5 mM MgCl2) supplemented with glycine (125 mM), followed by a second wash in TBS alone. Cells were resuspended in lysis buffer (50 mM HEPES [pH 7.5], 1 mM EDTA, 140 mM NaCl, 1% Triton X-100, 0.1% sodium deoxycholate, 1 mg/mL bacitracin, 1 mM benzamidine, and 1 mM PMSF). Glass beads were added to the cells suspension, followed by cell disruption in a bead beater for 6 min (1 min disruption each time with 2 min on-ice intervals). The cell lysate containing the genomic DNA was sheared to fragments with an average size of 0.5 kb by sonication (Bioruptor® Pico Sonicator B01080010). The cell debris was sedimented by centrifugation at 16,000×g for 20 min, and the collected supernatant was distributed into IP (Input) and Non-IP (Non-Input). For the IP samples, incubation was performed overnight with anti-c-Myc antibody (Sigma M4439) or anti-Rad51 antibody (a gift from Dr. Patrick Sung) at 4°C, followed by the addition of Dynabeads Protein G (Thermo, 1004D) and continued incubation for 4 h. Beads were then washed twice with lysis buffer, twice with high-salt lysis buffer (lysis buffer with 500 mM NaCl), twice with wash buffer (10 mM Tris-HCl [pH 8.0], 1 mM EDTA, 250 mM LiCl, 0.5% sodium deoxycholate, and 0.5% Igepal CA-630), and twice with 1× TE. DNA–protein complexes were eluted by incubating beads with 100 μL of elution buffer (50 mM Tris-HCl [pH 8.0], 10 mM EDTA, and 1% SDS) for 30 min at 65°C. Reverse cross-linking was carried out overnight at 65°C, followed by proteinase K treatment and phenol–chloroform purification of DNA. Purified DNA was analyzed by qPCR using the PowerUp SYBR Green Master Mix (Applied Biosystems, 4367659). Enrichment was normalized to the ACT1 locus. Accumulation of targeted proteins after DSB measured by ChIP is calculated by subtraction from before DSB.

## Round 1 — Reviewer Comments

### Reviewer 1

Liu et al. conducted a genome-wide screen to identify new break-induced replication (BIR) genes in yeast using an ectopic BIR assay with non-essential gene knockouts (KOs). This screen uncovered 37 novel BIR genes involved in various biological processes, including the spindle assembly checkpoint (SAC), the spindle position checkpoint (SPOC), nuclear pore/migration, and chromatin and post-translational modifications.
The study employs multiple assays, including another BIR assay (disomic assay) and the AMBER assay, to further validate and analyze the potential roles of SAC and SPOC in BIR. The authors also discuss the possible influence of epigenetic modifications of chromatin and nuclear pore components; however, these sections lack a clear mechanistic explanation, making them feel incomplete. It is somewhat surprising that so many pathways are interconnected with BIR, and many likely influence BIR indirectly by broadly regulating the cell cycle and stress responses. Nonetheless, the study is rigorous, employing multiple validation assays, and provides an initial framework for further exploration of this critical process in both yeast and human cells.
Key Questions and Considerations:
1. Can we test whether the prolonged duration of the current BIR system is responsible for its dependence on SAC? If we analyze BIR systems that require shorter DNA synthesis, as described by Symington or Haber, would BIR still be dependent on SAC or SPOC?
2. Can we distinguish whether the authors observed low cell viability or simply a prolonged cell cycle delay due to extended BIR in SPOC mutants?
3. Is the lethality of nup188 not offset by mad2 deletion because it may also be involved in the DNA damage response (DDR)? Is deletion of RAD9 partially rescue the low viability in nup188?
4. The discrepancy between BIR defects in mad2 using the disomic versus ectopic reporters is puzzling. The authors should resolve this inconsistency and ensure that candidate mutants showing BIR defects are consistently identified, regardless of the strain used to study BIR function.
5. Why is half crossover (HC) formation reduced in bub3 mutants?
6. The selection of 92 genes out of approximately 300 based solely on known gene function seems arbitrary. What criteria were used for this selection? The full list should be provided in the supplementary data.
7. Besides EAF3, did the screen identify any other genes that enhance BIR?
8. I noticed that HC formation is significantly increased in mad2 mutants. Can HC still generate Lys+ colonies in the ectopic assay?
9. In bub2 mutants, HC is not detected. What could be the underlying reason?

### Reviewer 2

Hiu et al. conducted a genetic screen focused on non-essential genes in budding yeast to identify factors mediating break-induced replication (BIR), a DNA repair pathway that can drive chromosome instability and contribute to tumorigenesis in mammals. The results present a list of 37 genes as novel candidate regulators of BIR-mediated repair. Most of the gene hits are known to be associated with or linked to diverse molecular pathways. The authors assessed the impact of many of these hits in various versions of BIR reporter assays, which included different genetic reporter assays and copy-number assessments targeting chromosomal regions proximal or distal to the DNA break site (serving as a readout of early vs. late BIR; or BIR initiation vs. BIR progression). Experiments involved evaluating the usage of BIR compared to other potential options (e.g., GC, HC, or CL), cell cycle progression, and cell viability. Overall, the authors draw several main conclusions: the Spindle Assembly Checkpoint (SAC) is required for BIR, the Spindle Position Checkpoint (SPOC) is necessary for BIR, Nuclear pore proteins (Nup84 vs. Nup188) have multiple roles in BIR, and various post-translational modifications are important for successful BIR repair.
Overall, the genetic screening conducted will interest researchers across various fields, including yeast genetics, checkpoint signaling, and genome stability. The authors deserve commendation for utilizing and clearly explaining several sophisticated genetic assays to evaluate BIR within different chromosomal contexts. However, this reviewer has several significant concerns that prevent the publication of this manuscript in its current form.
Major concerns:
The study is too preliminary and underdeveloped. In its present form, it may be better suited for a journal that reports genetic screen results without a significant level of mechanistic understanding or conceptual advance. However, as outlined below, these weaknesses may be addressable through a major revision.
Many unsubstantiated assumptions and speculations are made, leaving the data insufficient to support the claims. A significant weakness of the study is the interpretation of weak correlations as causations. The authors often conflate the effect of knocking out individual genes with the disruption of the known pathway where the gene product typically operates, and no robust experiments or controls are executed to establish strong causal relationships between the allegedly impacted pathway and the observed decrease in BIR.
Additionally, within each pathway claimed to be required for efficient BIR, how many non-essential genes exist in yeast, how many of those genes were identified as hits in the genetic screen, and how many have been evaluated in post-screen BIR validation assays? In other words, what percentage of non-essential genes linked to SAC, SPOC, NPCs, etc., are required for efficient BIR? Is the relationship between each of these sets of genes epistatic (e.g., BUB1, BUB3, and MAD2; Nup84 and Nup188; etc.) in terms of their effect on BIR?
How do the authors rule out the possibility that the proposed genes may impact BIR by operating independently of their known functions, such as through moonlighting-type roles? Similarly, additional molecular or cellular biological mechanistic insight would be beneficial. For instance, what is the exact molecular relationship between factors that regulate the proper attachment of microtubules to the kinetochore during mitosis and the supposedly prolonged G2/M arrest required for BIR repair? Which molecular steps of BIR-based repair rely on Nup84 versus Nup188, and why? How does this explain the apparent dependence on Nup84 for BIR initiation and on Nup188 for BIR completion? Overall, the authors could focus on providing further mechanistic insights related to a few of their numerous major claims to offer more robust support while possibly toning down other claims that lack detailed mechanistic/experimental insight.
Statistical analyses were often not depicted in the graphs (e.g., Fig. 1b, 2a,e-h, 3c-k, 4a-c,f-g, 5a-b,g-j, 6a,d-h) or may have been inappropriate. For instance, the supplemental table with the original results of the BIR screen (Supp Table 2) includes a t-test comparing all mutants to the WT. Since all mutants are compared to the same WT condition, the t-test is likely inappropriate and should be replaced with an ANOVA using multiple comparisons or a similar test that adjusts for multiple comparisons. Whether and how correcting the statistical analyses would change the list of screen hits identified and the overall results is a significant question. Additionally, the statistical analyses presented were sometimes unclear; for example, in Fig. 2d, was a Bonferroni correction or a similar adjustment applied for the multiple comparisons involving the WT condition?
Caution is advised when interpreting the knockout of a specific gene that affects BIR in only some of the BIR assays utilized. How might the specific chromosomal context of the reporter DSB assay influence the interpretation of these results?
Other point(s):
Although the text is well-written, a more thorough proofreading or professional English editing would significantly enhance the manuscript. A particularly frequent mistake was concerning the use of the definite article "the."
Given the important concerns outlined above, the manuscript's title and abstract could be misleading and should be revised with care.

### Reviewer 3

The manuscript by Liu, Lee et al represents a highly valuable addition to the understanding of the BIR process, a very important sub-pathway of homology-mediated repair of broken chromosomes. Defects in this process lead to the formation of structural genomic variants that are directly implicated in many disease processes. As noted by the authors, the number of cellular factors known to be involved in BIR is relatively limited, especially due to the lack of systematic efforts to identify them. This study is highly innovative in at least two ways. First, it reports on the results of such a systematic screen and uncovers dozens of new BIR factors, opening multiple exciting opportunities for follow-up research. Second, the authors present a comprehensive characterization of some of the most intriguing hits from their screen, in particular the genes involved in late cell cycle checkpoints (SAC and SPOC). The latter is very helpful in clarifying the relationship between the slow kinetics of BIR repair, and the need for fast-dividing cells to delay mitosis until BIR is completed. The authors also provide initial investigations of hits associated with the nuclear pore complex and chromatin structure, although not quite as in depth. Until now, studies of the BIR mechanism mostly focused on factors directly involved in DNA metabolism and repair (eg Pol32, Pif1, Rad51). Following this study, the range of cellular functions that will be investigated is expected to expand greatly, thus representing an influential contribution to the field.
Below are relatively minor comments, curiosities, suggestions that the authors and editors might wish to consider in a revised manuscript.
-The authors did a genomic (CHEF) analysis (Fig. 5) of the Leu- Ade+ clones derived from the nup mutants and showed that some of them were not regular BIR, but instead contained some GCRs. That analysis was quite informative, thus raising the question: Was this type of genomic analysis also done for the bub mutants (Fig. 2,3,4)? If not, should it be done? Given that the SAC and SPOC pathways were the major focus of the work following the screening phase, I think it might be important to add some information about this. In other words, how sure are the authors that Leu- Ade+ clones derived mutants such as bub2D or bfa1D actually mostly carry BIR products?
-Another aspect that I think should be commented on is the remarkable absence of half-crossovers (HC) in bub2D and nup184D. Both of these mutants displayed a massive drop in viability following DSB induction, and in both HCs were almost entirely gone. Is there a relationship? The authors included some discussion about gene conversions (GC), pointing out that GCs are in a “fast” repair class of products. HCs might also be in that “fast” repair group, so why are HCs gone while GCs increase (in bub2D)? I think this warrants some discussion.
-Finally, and not as relevant, I was a bit intrigued by the meaning of flower and bee in Figure 1e. I am not against it, but I did not find any comment in the manuscript or the figure legend to explain its meaning. I suggest the authors add some comment to provide context to the readers about why the diagram was drawn as such.

ectopic BIR system (YSJ131) (Supplementary Fig. 3a, b); however, mad2Δ and bub2Δ
were as proficient as WT at completing GC with copying ~5 kb in our allelic disomic
system in which the homology search between allelic locations is much faster (Fig. 2d,
Fig. 4d). The new data were added to Fig. 2b and to the Supplementary Fig. 3a-b, with
all raw data included in Supplementary Tables 2.2 and 2.3. Also, we added the following
sentences to the Results section:
• In support of this hypothesis, we observed a defective BIR in bub1Δ, bub3Δ, and
mad2Δ mutants in two ectopic BIR systems (AM3422 and YSJ131; Fig. 2 a, b;
Supplementary Fig. 3a, b, Supplementary Tables 2.1 and 2.2).
“However, in an ectopic system (YSJ133), where the homology search takes
longer and even GC can triggers checkpoint arrest BUB2 deletion led to a
modest decrease in GC efficiency (Supplementary Fig. 3b), but the defect of BIR
in this system (YSJ131) was more severe (Supplementary Fig. 3b).”
Reviewer 1, Comment 3. Can we distinguish whether the authors observed low cell
viability or simply a prolonged cell cycle delay due to extended BIR in SPOC mutants?
Reviewer 1, Response 3. To address this concern, we plated bfa1Δ and bub2Δ cells
on YEPD and YEP-Gal media and incubated the plates at 30 οC for 10 days. Cell
viability was calculated as the number of colonies formed on YEP-Gal over the number
of colonies formed on YEPD. Viability in bfa1Δ and bub2Δ cells after 10 days was low
and similar to viability previously observed after 5 days of growth. Importantly,
microscopic examination demonstrated that, among the cells that did not form colonies,
81% of bfa1Δ (34/42) and 47% of bub2Δ (26/55) cells stayed below the 4-cell stage.
Among the other plated cells that didn’t form colony, most divided fewer than 3 times,
and all of them contained fewer than 14 cells. Our results indicate that the low colony-
forming efficiency we observed following DSB induction in SPOC mutants results from
cell death rather than from slow growth associated with a prolonged cell cycle delay.
These data were added to Supplemental Fig. 3d, and the following sentence was added
to the Results section:
• “Microscopic examination demonstrated that, following plating on YEP-Gal
medium, most bub2Δ cells divided no more than twice, and no cells formed
micro-colonies after DSB induction (Supplementary Fig. 3d) confirming lethality
following the DSB.”
Reviewer 1, Comment 4. Is the lethality of nup188 not offset by mad2 deletion
because it may also be involved in the DNA damage response (DDR)? Is deletion of
RAD9 partially rescue the low viability in nup188?
additional experiments in nup188Δmad2Δ mutants of the disomic BIR strain. These
additional data allowed us to conclude that, following DSB induction, cell viability in the
double mutant is slightly but significantly increased as compared to nup188Δ alone (Fig.
5a).
Next, based on the Reviewer’s suggestion, we generated a nup188Δrad9Δ double
mutant in our chromosome III disomic BIR strain. After DSB induction in this strain, we
observed that RAD9 deletion partially rescued cell viability in the nup188Δ context (Fig.
5a). Unfortunately, we were unable to analyze the efficiency of BIR in
nup188Δmad2Δrad9Δ triple mutants because of their highly unstable (always
aneuploid) genomes. Collectively, our results lead us to propose that Nup188 can
participate in BIR through the interaction with DDC and SAC pathways.
These data were added to Fig. 5a-b, and the raw data were included in Supplementary
Table 4. In addition, we added the following sentence to the Results section:
• “Additional support came from the observation that deleting MAD2 or RAD9 in
nup188Δ significantly increased viability after DSB induction, albeit BIR remained
defective (based on the distribution of repair outcomes) (Fig. 5a-b,
Supplementary Fig. 6b, e, f).”
Reviewer 1, Comment 5. The discrepancy between BIR defects in mad2 using the
disomic versus ectopic reporters is puzzling. The authors should resolve this
inconsistency and ensure that candidate mutants showing BIR defects are consistently
identified, regardless of the strain used to study BIR function.
Reviewer 1, Response 5. To address this concern, we conducted several additional
biological repeats of the BIR assay in mad2Δ mutants of the ectopic BIR system
(AM3422). This allowed us to determine that MAD2 deletion mildly but significantly (by
individual Welch’s t-test) decreased BIR efficiency from 42% in WT to 37% in mad2Δ
(Fig. 2a), even though the one-way ANOVA test did not show significance
(Supplementary Table 2.1). Importantly, we also observed decreased BIR efficiency in
mad2Δ in an additional ectopic BIR system (YSJ131) by both Welch’s t-test and by
One-way ANOVA (Fig. 2b; Supplementary Table 2.2; see our response #2). In addition,
mad2Δ significantly decreased BIR in allelic BIR system (Fig. 2d). Thus, mad2Δ
significantly decreased BIR efficiency in two BIR systems, and the data were borderline
significant for the third system. We believe this borderline result could be explained by
our inability to distinguish BIR and half-crossovers in this ectopic system as Reviewer 1
suggested in comment 9.
Reviewer 1, Comment 6. Why is half crossover (HC) formation reduced in bub3
mutants?
Reviewer 1, Response 6. To address this, we performed several additional biological
repeats of these experiments, the results of which confirmed that the frequency of HCs
in bub3Δ is slightly but significantly lower compared to WT (Fig. 2d). We do not currently
have a clear explanation for this phenomenon. This lower frequency in bub3Δ could, in
3
principle, reflect the way that intermediates of unfinished BIR are resolved in these
mutants. We acknowledge that, while resolution of these intermediates can result in HC
formation, it can also lead to formation of outcomes indistinguishable from chromosome
loss (CL). It is also possible that HC events could undergo secondary strand invasion
and produce HC cascade events that would be phenotypically indistinguishable from
BIR. With our current data, it is hard to distinguish among these possibilities. Our results
in Fig. 2d have been updated with our new data.
Reviewer 1, Comment 7. The selection of 92 genes out of approximately 300 based
solely on known gene function seems arbitrary. What criteria were used for this
selection? The full list should be provided in the supplementary data.
Reviewer 1, Response 7. Out of 335 candidate BIR genes identified in our screen,
243 genes were excluded from further investigation. The list of excluded genes
includes:
1) 28 genes that were known to be false positives, including:
a. 10 genes located on chromosome V between CAN1 and the telomere,
which appeared as false positives on our candidate gene list because
selection of mutant of these genes will against the selection of the BIR
chromosome.
b. 18 genes involved in lysine biosynthesis, which represent false positives
because our BIR assay was based on Lys+ selection.
2) 19 BIR genes that were previously described, and, therefore, deprioritized for our
current study.
3) Because our study aimed to identify genes directly involved in BIR occurring
within the nucleus, we excluded 193 genes that have no known role in DNA
metabolism, including:
a. 132 genes with mitochondrial or metabolism/biosynthetic roles,
b. 28 genes involved in transcription or RNA metabolism,
c. 20 genes that control ribosome- or endoplasmic reticulum-related
functions, and
d. 13 genes with unknown functions
e. 3 other genes involved in cell cycle regulation
In response to this Reviewer’s comment, the full list of genes identified from the screen
and whether they were included in or excluded from further analysis was incorporated
into Supplementary Table 3, with the reasoning behind the exclusion of some genes
included in the table legend. In addition, to clarify the criteria used to select 92 genes for
further analysis, the Results section was corrected as follows:
• “We identified 335 KO strains (Supplementary Table 3) with fewer Lys+ papillae
compared to WT, 19 of which (e.g. RAD52, RAD51, POL32, SRS2, RAD54;)
were already known to promote BIR. From the rest, 92 genes were selected for
further characterization based on their known roles in processes related to DNA
metabolism, including, for example spindle checkpoints, nucleopore structure,
and post-translational modification of proteins associated with DNA
4
(Supplementary Table 3.1). The other identified genes, including mitochondrial
and metabolism/biosynthetic genes (Supplementary Table 3.2), were expected to
affect BIR indirectly, and, therefore, were not prioritized in this study. “
Reviewer 1, Comment 8. Besides EAF3, did the screen identify any other genes that
enhance BIR?
Reviewer 1, Response 8. Yes, our screen identified 6 genes for which BIR efficiency
was increased upon their deletion: UBA3, UBA4, MUB1, CCS1, YVH1, and PIB2
(Supplementary Table 2.1 and 2.3). To address this Reviewer’s concern, these genes
are listed in the Results section:
• “Interestingly, deletions of the remaining 6 genes (UBA3, UBA4, MUB1, CCS1,
YVH1, and PIB21) resulted in increased BIR efficiency, suggesting these genes
represent BIR suppressors; however, these genes were probably selected by our
screen due to conferring a slow-growth phenotype (Supplementary Table 3).”
Reviewer 1, Comment 9. I noticed that HC formation is significantly increased in
mad2 mutants. Can HC still generate Lys+ colonies in the ectopic assay?
Reviewer 1, Response 9. We thank the Reviewer for this comment. We agree that,
because all BIR occurs during G2 (a two-chromatid stage of the cell cycle), an HC that
formed in our ectopic system followed by co-segregation of an HC product with a
second copy of an intact donor would produce an outcome indistinguishable from BIR.
While, in the allelic BIR system, HCs (at least a half of them) can be readily
distinguished from BIR, no such distinction can be made in the ectopic BIR system.
We are not sure why mad2Δ leads to a small but significant increase in HCs, but this
observation may explain why it was so difficult to detect the decrease in BIR in mad2Δ
mutants in the ectopic system; specifically, HCs were likely counted as BIR events in the
ectopic system.
Reviewer 1, Comment 10. In bub2 mutants, HC is not detected. What could be the
underlying reason?
Reviewer 1, Response 10. We reported here that, in the absence of Bub2, the majority
of cells undergoing BIR die due to the onset of cytokinesis in cells where nuclear
division is delayed; only a very small portion of BIR outcomes—likely those that
complete repair before the onset of dysregulated cytokinesis—form colonies. This result
predicts that anything that delays or interrupts BIR would promote cell death in bub2∆
cells. The formation of HCs is likely associated with delays during BIR repair, such as
pausing, interruption, resolution of BIR intermediates, or formation of a secondary DSB
(breakage of the BIR donor chromosome), which could extend nuclear division arrest.
Therefore, it is expected that no HC events would complete before the onset of
cytokinesis, because any bub2∆ cells in the process of forming an HC would have
extended nuclear arrest resulting in cell death. To address this comment in the revised
manuscript, we included the following sentence in the Results section:
5
• “The fraction of HC outcomes among survivors was very low in bub2Δ and bfa1Δ
mutants (Fig. 4d), likely because of the extended time required for HC formation,
which involves secondary breakage of the donor chromosome. Collectively, these
results support that the viability of cells undergoing BIR depends on the SPOC.
Reviewer #2 (Remarks to the Author):
Reviewer 2, Comment 11. Many unsubstantiated assumptions and speculations are
made, leaving the data insufficient to support the claims. A significant weakness of the
study is the interpretation of weak correlations as causations. The authors often conflate
the effect of knocking out individual genes with the disruption of the known pathway
where the gene product typically operates, and no robust experiments or controls are
executed to establish strong causal relationships between the allegedly impacted
pathway and the observed decrease in BIR.
Reviewer 2, Response 11. Our study reports a genome-wide screen wherein we
identified 335 gene candidates involved in BIR, and we confirmed the roles of 30
genes—grouped into 5 functional groups/pathways according to their known functions—
in BIR using multiple BIR experimental systems. Because of the scope of our findings, it
was necessary to prioritize particular genes, which we did based on our expectation that
certain genes might be more likely to uncover clear molecular pathways that contribute
to the efficiency of BIR. To address this Reviewer’s concern, we performed additional
experiments to elucidate the role of three of the pathways we identified in this study: (i)
the SAC pathway, ii) the SPOC pathway, and (iii) the nucleopore complex. The following
new experiments were conducted:
1. We conducted a series of new cytological experiments to analyze BIR repair in
two additional SAC mutant lines: bfa1Δ and bub2Δmad2Δ. These experiments
demonstrated that, similarly to bub2Δ, only a small fraction (7%) of bfa1Δ cells
successfully formed colonies (Fig. 4c, Supplementary Table 4), while the vast
majority of cells formed cell chains with anucleate cells (Fig. 4f, g, j; see
Supplementary Table 7 for all raw data), indicative of cytokinesis onset prior to
nuclear division and BIR completion. In bub2Δmad2Δ, the fraction of anucleate
cells forming chains was decreased compared to bub2Δ (Fig. 4h, j; see
Supplementary Table 7 for all raw data), and a significant fraction of bub2Δmad2Δ
cells demonstrated earlier recovery from nuclear checkpoint arrest due to
absence of the SAC consistent with the increased viability of the double mutant as
compared to bub2Δ.
2. We performed an epistasis analysis involving SAC and SPOC mutants and
determined the effects of double mutations on BIR efficiency. These experiments
showed that the low viability of SPOC mutants after DSB induction could be
rescued by deactivation of the SAC pathway. In particular, the viability of
bub2Δmad2Δ cells was increased compared to bub2Δ cells (Fig. 4c,
Supplementary Table 4), which supported our hypothesis that discoordination
between nuclear division (following nuclear division arrest) and the onset of
cytokinesis underlies the observed lethality in SPOC mutants after DSB induction.
In addition, we observed that BUB1 is epistatic to MAD2 with respect to BIR
6
efficiency (Fig. 2d; Supplementary Fig. 4a, h; Supplementary Table 4), consistent
with MAD2 and BUB1 functioning in the same (SAC) pathway during BIR.
3. We performed several detailed analyses of the roles of Nup84 and Nup188 in
BIR. (1) Using chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP), we now demonstrate that
both Nup84 and Nup188 localize to the DSB (Fig. 5g). (2) We also performed
ChIP using an anti-Rad51 antibody, which demonstrated that the absence of
Nup84 does not affect Rad51 loading at the DSB site of the broken (recipient)
chromosome (Fig. 5h). Further, we observed that Rad51 loading on the donor
chromosome (reflecting strand invasion) was reduced in nup84∆ compared to wild
type cells, however, a substantial level of Rad51 loading on the donor was
observed even in the absence of Nup84 (Fig. 5h). Given our observation that the
initiation of BIR synthesis was defective in nup84Δ mutants, we propose that
Nup84 facilitates strand invasion, and it plays a particularly important role after
strand invasion and before initiation of BIR synthesis. For example, Nup84 may
be important for the formation and stabilization (maturation) of the D-loop or
initiation of BIR synthesis (possibly by facilitating the recruitment of Rad54, PCNA,
DNA polymerases, or Pif1 helicases). (4) We now demonstrate that nup84Δ is
epistatic to nup188Δ with respect to BIR efficiency and cell viability after DSB
induction (Fig. 5a, b), supporting our model wherein Nup84 functions prior to
Nup188. (5) In addition, our genetic analysis of BIR efficiency and cell viability
after DSB induction in nup188Δmad2Δ and nup188Δrad9Δ double mutants
suggested a potential role for Nup188 in checkpoint control during DSB repair,
which is a novel finding (Fig. 5a, b).
4. We introduced deletions of 30 newly identified BIR genes in an additional BIR
experimental system (YSJ131; see our response #18) (Supplementary Table 2.2,
and we tested the effects of several mutations in the GC ectopic system (see our
response #2), which provided additional mechanistic insights (Supplementary
Table 2.3).
All of these new results are included in the Results section of the revised manuscript
and discussed in the revised Discussion section.
Reviewer 2, Comment 12. Additionally, within each pathway claimed to be required for
efficient BIR, how many non-essential genes exist in yeast, how many of those genes
were identified as hits in the genetic screen, and how many have been evaluated in
post-screen BIR validation assays? In other words, what percentage of non-essential
genes linked to SAC, SPOC, NPCs, etc., are required for efficient BIR?
Reviewer 2, Response 12. Based on the literature, there are 5 non-essential SAC
genes (HOYT et al. 1991; LI AND MURRAY 1991; WEISS AND WINEY 1996), and our screen
successfully identified two: BUB1 and BUB3. Further analysis revealed that deletion of
MAD2 also reduced BIR efficiency from 42% in wild type cells to 37% (based on the
individual Welch’s t-test) in the ectopic BIR system (AM3422). This modest reduction
may explain why MAD2 was not identified in our initial screen (a discussion of this
phenotype is provided in our response #9). Thus, the three main proteins known to
cooperate to execute the SAC are all important for BIR. We also tested mad3Δ mutants,
which showed no effect on BIR. Interestingly, deletion of MAD1 significantly increased
BIR efficiency in our ectopic assay (Supplementary Table 2.1). It was previously
7
demonstrated that Mad1 functions as a scaffold to recruit Mad2 to the kinetochore, but
the function of Mad2 in suppressing APC can be Mad1 independent. Therefore, it is
possible that transducing signals to SAC during BIR bears some unique features that
are not yet understood.
For the SPOC pathway, 7 of 10 genes are non-essential, as described in (CAYDASI et al.
2010). Our study identified two of them, BUB2 and BFA1, as BIR genes (Fig. 4), In
addition, we identified three genes involved in nuclear migration (Supplementary Fig.
3f), including JNM1, as well as components of the dynein pathway (NUM1 and APR1)—
both of which are functionally related to the SPOC—and our post-screen BIR validation
assays demonstrated that they were all involved in BIR.
Similarly, 17 out of 31 subunits of the nuclear pore complex (NPC) are non-
essential(HAMED AND ANTONIN 2021). Our screen only identified NUP188—a non-
essential gene—while our further experiments also confirmed Nup84 as an important
BIR protein (Fig. 5).
Reviewer 2, Comment 13. Is the relationship between each of these sets of genes
epistatic (e.g., BUB1, BUB3, and MAD2; Nup84 and Nup188; etc.) in terms of their
effect on BIR?
Reviewer 2, Response 13. To address this question, we constructed bub1Δmad2Δ
double mutants and tested BIR efficiency. The double mutant had a BIR defect that was
similar to the defect observed in each of the single mutants, suggesting that BUB1 and
MAD2 are epistatic and act in the same pathway during BIR (Fig. 2d; Supplementary
Fig. 4a, h; Supplementary Table 4).
We also generated a nup188Δnup84Δ double mutants, and we found that the double
mutants had increased cell viability after DSB induction compared to nup188Δ single
mutants (Fig. 5a). Together with our other genetic and kinetics studies, this result
supported our initial hypothesis that NUP188 and NUP84 operate at different stages of
BIR, with Nup84 acting during earlier steps while Nup188 contributes to the successful
completion of BIR.
In response to this comment, several figure panels were created or changed including
Fig. 2d, Fig. 5a,b, Supplementary Fig. 4a, h, and Supplementary Fig. 6b, g of the
revised manuscript, and the following sentences were added in the Results section:
• “In addition, bub1∆mad2∆ double mutants showed a BIR defect similar to each
single mutant (Fig. 2d; Supplementary Fig. 4a, h).”
• “We found that nup188Δnup84Δ double mutants had higher viability than
nup188∆ (78% vs 12%, respectively) (Fig. 5a) and an altered distribution of DSB
repair outcomes (Fig. 5b, Supplementary Fig. 6b, g), supporting our hypothesis
that Nup188 participates later than Nup84 in BIR.”
genes may impact BIR by operating independently of their known functions, such as
through moonlighting-type roles?
Reviewer 2, Response 14. We acknowledge it is difficult to completely rule out that
some of our newly identified genes impact BIR independently of their known primary
functions, especially when dealing with more than 30 new genes that we characterized.
While it will take many more years and laboratories to delineate the precise molecular
roles of each of our newly identified genes, we think that the following arguments can be
made:
1. The strength of our study, in our opinion, is that we were able to discover the
roles of several members of the same functional group within BIR. Examples
include SAC, SPOC, NPC, and several chromatin remodeling proteins. When
several proteins from a functional group are confirmed to affect BIR efficiency, we
think it provides support for the idea that the whole pathway participates in BIR,
and this makes it more likely that the identified proteins are cooperating to exert
their known related functions, rather than by moonlighting in BIR.
2. The functions of the DDC, SAC, and SPOC in BIR are supported by various
methods, including genetic, molecular biological, and cytological experiments,
which together support our hypotheses that the DDC and SAC are required to
prevent nuclear divisions prior to BIR completion, while the SPOC is required to
prevent premature cytokinesis before nuclear division. The phenotypes observed
in our BIR studies (especially those observed cytologically) are consistent with
these pathways playing their main roles in cell cycle regulation. Genetic
interactions between mutants from these three groups also support this idea.
3. Our data obtained for Nup84 and Nup188 also suggest a direct role of the NPC
in facilitating DSB repair through BIR. Our new ChIP data demonstrate that these
proteins directly interact with broken DNA, consistent with previous findings that
DNA fragile sites relocalize to the nuclear pore during DNA replication/repair to
ensure accurate synthesis and genomic stability.
Reviewer 2, Comment 15. Similarly, additional molecular or cellular biological
mechanistic insight would be beneficial. For instance, what is the exact molecular
relationship between factors that regulate the proper attachment of microtubules to the
kinetochore during mitosis and the supposedly prolonged G2/M arrest required for BIR
repair?
Reviewer 2, Response 15.
To address this Reviewer’s question, we hypothesized that, similar to (DOTIWALA et al.
2010; ZHOU et al. 2024), the initiation of a DSB at MAT should be followed by spreading
of γH2Ax across a large chromosomal region and reach the centromere, which initiates
detachment of microtubules from the centromere. This was proposed to activate the
SAC in response to the DSB (DOTIWALA et al. 2010; ZHOU et al. 2024). To test this, we
introduced the hta1-S129A and hta2∆ double mutations in our disomic system to
eliminate the ability of histone H2A to undergo γH2Ax modification. These mutations
9
caused a significant but very mild BIR defect, which was much less severe than the
defects we observed in strains with BUB1, BUB3 or MAD2 deletions (Supplementary
Table 4). Therefore, an alternative mechanism might activate the SAC during BIR. It is
interesting, in this regard, that our results described in response #12 demonstrated that,
while Bub1, Bub3, and Mad2 were required for successful BIR, MAD1 deletion led to
increased BIR efficiency (Supplementary Table 2.1). Because Mad1 is known to function
as a scaffold for the recruitment of Mad2 to the kinetochore in response to a lack of
microtubule attachment, it is possible that transduction of the signal to the SAC is
independent of microtubule attachment to the kinetochore. To this end, we are now
examining whether SAC activation during BIR might be dependent on Tel1 and Mec1,
but independent of the kinetochore, which has been proposed previously (KIM AND
BURKE 2008). Also, we are exploring the interplay between DSBs at MAT and
detachment of microtubes from the centromere using a combination of genetic and
molecular biological approaches. All these experiments are expected to take a
significant amount of time and will be described in a future publication.
To address this issue in the revised manuscript, we added the following statement to the
Discussion section:
“For unrepairable breaks, it was established that activation of the SAC proceeds by the
spreading of γH2AX from the DSB to the centromere on the broken chromosome,
causing kinetochore dysfunction and prolonging G2/M arrest. However, we observed
that in our allelic BIR system, an H2A-S129A mutant defective for γH2AX modification
exhibited only a minor BIR defect, which was much less severe than the defect
observed in SAC mutants (Supplementary Table 4). Therefore, an alternative
mechanism may activate the SAC during BIR. For example, previous studies have
demonstrated that SAC activation could be achieved in a Tel1- and Mec1-dependent but
kinetochore-independent manner."
Reviewer 2, Comment 16. Which molecular steps of BIR-based repair rely on Nup84
versus Nup188, and why? How does this explain the apparent dependence on Nup84
for BIR initiation and on Nup188 for BIR completion? Overall, the authors could focus on
providing further mechanistic insights related to a few of their numerous major claims to
offer more robust support while possibly toning down other claims that lack detailed
mechanistic/experimental insight.
Reviewer 2, Response 16. To address this question, we conducted ChIP, which
showed that both Nup84 and Nup188 participate in DSB repair by physically interacting
with broken DNA ends (Fig. 5g). We also found that Nup84 and Nup188 act sequentially
during BIR, with Nup84 participating in earlier steps and Nup188 near the end. In
addition, we used the AMBER methodology, which showed no initiation of BIR synthesis
in the absence of Nup84 (Fig. 5e; Supplementary Fig. 6h). Moreover, Rad51 ChIP in
nup84∆ cells demonstrated wild-type levels of Rad51 loaded onto the broken
chromosome, and a decreased but still substantial amount of Rad51 loaded on the
donor chromosome (Fig. 5h). This suggests that the absence of Nup84 did not affect
DSB resection but partially impaired strand invasion and results in a critical defect in the
step following strand invasion. Altogether, our new data allowed us to pinpoint when
Nup84 acts during BIR: we now think that it helps during strand invasion and also plays
an essential role after strand invasion and prior to the initiation of BIR synthesis. From
10
these data, we propose that Nup84 could be important for recruiting BIR proteins, such
as Rad54, Pif1, PCNA, or DNA polymerases, during D-loop stabilization and initiation of
BIR synthesis.
Further, our new data support that Nup188 acts later during BIR than Nup84.
First,
AMBER demonstrated that, in the absence of Nup188, BIR synthesis can initiate but
becomes very defective towards its end (Fig. 5f; Supplementary Fig. 6h). Second,
deleting NUP84 in nup188Δ cells restored viability after DSB induction (Fig. 5a),
which
suggested that the cell death observed in nup188Δ mutants resulted from formation of
BIR intermediates mediated by Nup84. In addition, previous studies reported that
hNUP188 interacts with the SAC and plays a role in regulating centrosome formation,
indicating that yeast Nup188 could also play a role in checkpoint establishment during
BIR. In support of this, our new genetic data demonstrate that inactivation of the SAC or
DDC partially rescues cell viability following DSB induction in nup188Δ (Fig. 5a).
In response to this comment, we added new genetics data to Figures 5a and 5b and
ChIP data to Figures 5g and 5h. We also re-wrote the entire sections in the Results and
Discussion dedicated to nuclear pore proteins.
Reviewer 2, Comment 17. Statistical analyses were often not depicted in the graphs
(e.g., Fig. 1b, 2a,e-h, 3c-k, 4a-c,f-g, 5a-b,g-j, 6a,d-h) or may have been inappropriate.
For instance, the supplemental table with the original results of the BIR screen (Supp
Table 2) includes a t-test comparing all mutants to the WT. Since all mutants are
compared to the same WT condition, the t-test is likely inappropriate and should be
replaced with an ANOVA using multiple comparisons or a similar test that adjusts for
multiple comparisons. Whether and how correcting the statistical analyses would
change the list of screen hits identified and the overall results is a significant question.
Additionally, the statistical analyses presented were sometimes unclear; for example, in
Fig. 2d, was a Bonferroni correction or a similar adjustment applied for the multiple
comparisons involving the WT condition?
Reviewer 2, Response 17. In response to this comment, we took the following steps.
First, we ensured that every figure and legend (including those indicated by the
reviewer) contains details of the statistical analyses.
Second, we updated the statistical methods to account for multiple hypothesis testing,
as suggested. Specifically, for the viability assays we now use one-way ANOVA (with
Dunnett’s post-hoc test, grouping all mutants tested in each system). We included the
P-values from both the one-way ANOVA and the Welch’s t-test in Supplementary
Tables 2.1 and 2.2. For the BIR repair distribution assays, we applied the Benjamini–
Hochberg correction (with a false discovery rate of 0.05, grouping all mutants tested in
each system) to the existing Chi-square test.
Importantly, the vast majority of mutants that were previously shown to have significant
defects remained significantly defective based on the results obtained using these
updated statistical methods. For several mutants that were only nominally significant
(significant before correction but not after), we updated the figures, tables, and text to
11
correctly reflect their defectiveness. Two of these mutants (bub1Δ and mad2Δ) remain
on the list of our BIR players as they were defective in 2 of our 3 BIR systems (YSJ131
and AM1411) for plating outcomes. In addition, their BIR defect is supported by our
ddPCR-based AMBER method and by cytological studies. Thus, we believe it is
essential to continue research even on mutants demonstrating modest defects by
plating genetics, as they may uncover important mechanistic insights during the process
of BIR and DNA repair.
Reviewer 2, Comment 18. Caution is advised when interpreting the knockout of a
specific gene that affects BIR in only some of the BIR assays utilized. How might the
specific chromosomal context of the reporter DSB assay influence the interpretation of
these results?
Reviewer 2, Response 18. In our original manuscript, we verified 33 individual BIR
candidate genes in our ectopic BIR strain (AM3422), and we also deleted many of these
genes in the disomic strain (allelic BIR system, AM1411) (Supplementary Table 4).
These BIR systems differ in several ways. First, in both systems, DSBs are induced in
different chromosomes and repaired by ectopic BIR in the first system and by allelic BIR
in the second one. In response to this reviewer’s question, we introduced deletions of
24 genes into a third, ectopic BIR system (YSJ131), which we received from Dr. James
Haber (Supplementary Table 2.2). This BIR system was constructed in a different

mediated repair of broken chromosomes. Defects in this process lead to the formation

As noted by the authors, the number of cellular factors known to be involved in BIR is
relatively limited, especially due to the lack of systematic efforts to identify them. This
study is highly innovative in at least two ways. First, it reports on the results of such a
systematic screen and uncovers dozens of new BIR factors, opening multiple exciting
opportunities for follow-up research. Second, the authors present a comprehensive
characterization of some of the most intriguing hits from their screen, in particular the
genes involved in late cell cycle checkpoints (SAC and SPOC). The latter is very helpful
in clarifying the relationship between the slow kinetics of BIR repair, and the need for
fast-dividing cells to delay mitosis until BIR is completed. The authors also provide initial
investigations of hits associated with the nuclear pore complex and chromatin structure,
although not quite as in depth. Until now, studies of the BIR mechanism mostly focused
on factors directly involved in DNA metabolism and repair (eg Pol32, Pif1, Rad51).
Following this study, the range of cellular functions that will be investigated is expected
to expand greatly, thus representing an influential contribution to the field.

Reviewer 3, Comment 22. Another aspect that I think should be commented on is the
remarkable absence of half-crossovers (HC) in bub2D and nup184D. Both of these
mutants displayed a massive drop in viability following DSB induction, and in both HCs
were almost entirely gone. Is there a relationship? The authors included some
discussion about gene conversions (GC), pointing out that GCs are in a “fast” repair
13
class of products. HCs might also be in that “fast” repair group, so why are HCs gone
while GCs increase (in bub2D)? I think this warrants some discussion.
Reviewer 3, Response 22. We thank the reviewer for this insight. As we mentioned in
our response #10, we predicted that any delay or interruption of BIR should promote cell
death in the absence of Bub2. The formation of HCs is likely associated with additional
delays during BIR, such as BIR pausing, interruption, resolution of BIR intermediates,
and a secondary DSB (breakage of BIR donor), which could extend nuclear division
arrest. Therefore, we would expect that HC events would not complete before the onset
of cytokinesis and would instead be associated with cell death. We believe that the
absence of HCs in nup188∆ mutants (we believe this is the gene the reviewer intended,
versus NUP184) could be explained in a similar way, which is supported by our new
observation that mad2Δ and rad9Δ partially suppress cell lethality after DSB initiation in
cells lacking Nup188 (Fig. 5a).
In response to this comment, we included the following sentence in our Results section:
• “The fraction of HC outcomes among survivors was very low in bub2Δ and bfa1Δ
mutants (Fig. 4d), likely because of the extended time required for HC formation,
which involves secondary breakage of the donor chromosome.”
